#9841. 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:

The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:

Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

#9840. Fig Announces Elastic Integration to Help Security Teams Protect Detection Coverage as Data Changes

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Fig announced an integration partnership with Elastic on November 19, 2026, the company said in a press release. Fig helps security operations (SecOps) engineers map detection dependencies, identify breaks and validate changes before they reach production. The integration connects Fig with Elastic Security, which Elastic describes as an open, agentic security operations platform. It is designed to let security teams build, ship and run detection and response while seeing how changes to their data affect what they can detect.

First reported by SiliconANGLE, the partnership deals with a practical concern for organizations that rely on detection rules to flag suspicious activity. Those rules work only when the data feeding them arrives in the structure they expect, and that structure can shift over time. Fig and Elastic link upstream data changes to the downstream detections that rely on them, which gives engineers control over each change that touches security coverage.

Elastic Security gives customers a starting point through prebuilt integrations and detection rules that help establish coverage from day one. Fig picks up from there and helps SecOps engineers safeguard and expand that coverage as their environments evolve. Elastic Security supplies the platform and its prebuilt content, and Fig focuses on the dependencies that tie upstream data changes to the detections built on that data.

Gal Shafir, co-founder and chief executive officer of Fig, summed up how the two companies divide the work. "Elastic gives security teams control over their data, and Fig gives them control over the engineering around it," Shafir said.

Detection rules depend on specific fields and values to recognize an attack. A vendor may update its log format, a team may bring a new source online, or an upstream pipeline may be reshaped to manage cost and performance. In each case, the information a rule needs may stop arriving in the form it expects. These changes may be intentional and beneficial, but they often happen in tools owned by different teams.

The result is drift. Data keeps flowing and rules stay active, yet a rule can lose the information it needs to catch the attacks it was written to detect. The partnership is designed to help Elastic users understand these dependencies, identify where a change has affected detection coverage and follow a clearer path from discovering an issue to addressing its cause.

Fig connects to Elastic through a read-only application programming interface (API) key and retrieves the configuration of the Elastic environment. From that configuration, Fig's deterministic Security Data Lineage maps each source through pipelines, mappings and fields to the detection rules that use them.

With that map in place, engineers can see what each rule relies on before a change goes live. When a source, pipeline or mapping changes, Fig identifies the affected detections, pinpoints where the flow broke and recommends a fix. Engineers can then use that context to investigate the issue and assess the proposed repair.

Jamie Hynds, director of product at Elastic, explained the value from Elastic's side of the partnership. "Environments never stop changing, from vendor schemas and APIs to ETL tools and pipelines. Fig traces those changes to the detection rules that depend on them, so SecOps teams can adapt quickly and maintain detection coverage with Elastic Security," Hynds said. ETL stands for extract, transform and load.

Elastic's prebuilt integrations and research-backed detection rules provide broad coverage out of the box. Elastic's Automatic Import feature and its artificial intelligence (AI) Agent help teams build new integrations and custom rules as their requirements grow. Fig works alongside those capabilities by testing changes against the organization's own data and environment context before anything reaches production.

Once a change is validated, engineers can ship it as code using continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD), with version control and one-click rollback. Taken together, these steps form an engineering workflow that ties each planned change to its expected effect on detection coverage. Teams can assess dependencies, test adjustments and manage deployment as they add sources, refine pipelines or expand use cases. Shafir presented that workflow as a way to keep pace without giving up visibility. "Teams can see how every source connects to every detection, test each change against their own environment and ship it as code. That lets them move quickly without losing sight of their coverage," he said.

The integration also covers platform migrations. For organizations moving from another security information and event management (SIEM) platform, Elastic's Automatic Migration translates existing detection rules. Fig then checks each translated rule against the data available in Elastic before cutover, flags rules that need rework and recommends fixes. This validation helps engineers see where translated detection logic and the destination environment's data need to be aligned before switching over. Existing Elastic users can apply the same checks when they introduce sources or change detection use cases.

#9839. What Is Host Header Injection? Detection to Exploitation with Burp

Posted on Nov 19 • Originally published at eminuzun.com

There's a small line inside every HTTP request: the "Host" header.

When your browser goes to a site, it tells the server "this is where I've come." Since hundreds of sites can live on a single server, the server figures out which one you want from this line.

But some applications trust this header too much.

The Host header is entirely under the user's control. If you want, you write your own domain there, and the server takes it as correct and uses it. That's exactly where Host Header Injection begins.

So where does the application get into danger when it uses this header? The most classic spot is password reset.

You forgot your password, so you click "reset my password." The server sends you an email with a link in it. Where does it get that link's domain from? Some applications pull their own address from the Host header.

If the attacker points Host to their own server, the reset link goes to their server too.

Burp Suite is all you need to see this flaw. I'll show it on the Basic password reset poisoning lab from PortSwigger Web Security Academy.

In the lab, our victim is "carlos." The task is to take over his account. It also gives you an "exploit server."

First you go to the login page and click "Forgot password?". You type carlos's username and send the request.

You send the request to Repeater, because there you can easily change the Host header and try again and again.

You find the Host line. It shows the lab's own address.

There's a small trap here. Modern labs send the request as HTTP/2. In HTTP/2 the host information isn't in the normal Host: line but in the hidden :authority field. So if you only change the Host line, you may get a 400 saying Host header not present.

In Repeater, switch the HTTP version to HTTP/1 from the settings icon at the top right of the request. Now the Host line works normally.

One more warning: write only the hostname in the Host value. Don't add things like "https://" at the start or "/exploit" at the end, or it's treated as invalid again.

You delete the Host line and write the exploit server's address.

The server returns 200. It accepted the request.

What happens in the background? The server sends a reset email to the user carlos and takes the link's domain from the Host we wrote. So the link now points to our exploit server.

carlos opens that email and clicks the link (the lab simulates this automatically). The moment he clicks, the reset token lands on our server.

Where do we see the token? In the exploit server's access log.

In the log you see carlos's GET request and the token in it. This token is the key to the reset page.

Now you take that token and paste it into the normal reset link. In the form that opens, you can change carlos's password.

The token worked and the password was changed.

That's really all there is to the detection part. All you do is change the Host header and check whether the response or the application's behavior changes. If it shows up on the page or makes it into the email link, there's a flaw.

Also, some applications filter Host but forget the "X-Forwarded-Host" header. So if Host doesn't work, try adding this to the request.

Often the filter checks Host but not this header, and the same flaw can be sitting there.

As for protection, the server should never take its absolute address from the Host header. It should keep a fixed list of domains or read it from configuration. You can't trust a header the user sends.

Originally written in Turkish on eminuzun.com. AI was used only for the translation.

#9838. Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases

Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them

Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:

Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:

-Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

-Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

-Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:

Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

Explore the models on Confluent to see how time-series intelligence can support real-time decisions.

#9837. Converting iPhone HEVC Videos for Telegram Video Avatars with ffmpeg

I built a small Telegram bot for video avatars, and the first bug I hit was a silent failure. Some iPhone videos upload fine, Telegram accepts the file, and then nothing happens. No error message.

Most iPhones record in HEVC (H.265) inside a .MOV container by default. Telegram's video avatar pipeline expects H.264 in an MP4. The upload succeeds, so there's no error to catch, and the avatar just never updates.

I spent an evening assuming my code was wrong before I ran ffprobe on the file:

That hevc line was the whole story. The file was 1920x1080 landscape too, which is a second problem, since the avatar needs a square.

These are the constraints I target, based on what I've seen work:

Telegram doesn't document all of this in one place, so treat the numbers as what I've confirmed in testing, not a spec I'm quoting. If Telegram changes the limits, the bot will need an update.

The conversion runs in two passes. The first pass finds the crop rectangle from the first 10 seconds. The second pass crops, scales, strips audio, and encodes.

If the output comes out over 2 MB, I bump -crf by 2 and encode again. In my tests a 10-second clip at crf 26 usually lands between 600 KB and 1.2 MB, so the retry rarely fires. It exists for high-motion footage.

Here's the bot side, trimmed to the parts that matter. It downloads the upload, converts it with the same two ffmpeg passes, and sends the result back.

The handler runs ffmpeg inline, so one slow conversion blocks nothing else, but a burst of uploads does pile up CPU. I haven't added a queue yet.

The handler above is most of the bot. The rest is a database for usage counts, a size check before download, and a message when the clip is too long. I put it up as @LiveAvaBot so people could try it without installing ffmpeg.

The numbers after roughly three weeks: 534 users total, 5 new users in the last 24 hours, 3 conversions in the same window, and zero Stars revenue in 24 hours. The conversion rate is low, and I don't yet know whether that's the onboarding message, the 10-second limit, or simply that most people who find the bot don't have a broken HEVC clip to fix.

The biggest lesson is to check the codec before you debug your code. Half my time went into reading my own handler when one ffprobe line would have pointed at the problem.

Next I want to test the output on older Telegram clients and add a queue so bursts don't stall the worker.

#9836. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9835. Three Records Your Support Team Needs After a Background Job Fails

Fractional CTO in Ilford, UK. Co-Founder, CTO and COO at AlphaRages.

Fractional CTO in Ilford, UK. Co-Founder, CTO and COO at AlphaRages.

Fractional CTO in Ilford, UK. Co-Founder, CTO and COO at AlphaRages.

Conceptual recovery view. The lab stores accepted input and row results and derives the outcome; recovery-owner tracking is not implemented. Catalog data is fictional; the code and process-exit tests ran locally.

When a customer asks whether to upload a failed import again, the worker's health check cannot tell support what already changed. A retry count cannot answer that question either. The useful evidence is the accepted input, the committed work and the outcome derived from those records.

Here is a runnable catalog importer that makes those questions inspectable. The supplier and product data are fictional. The local implementation and failure tests were executed with Python 3.13.3 and SQLite 3.49.2; they are not a customer deployment or a distributed-system benchmark.

The lab uses one supplier's catalog in one disposable SQLite file. It deliberately keeps the catalog update and the completed-row result in the same database. There is no queue or external inventory API.

Save the three files in the appendix together: importer.py, test_importer.py and sample.json. Python's standard library supplies all dependencies. Use a new disposable database, never a production or shared one. From that directory, run:

The captured implementation suite passed all four tests. The version command lets you record your own environment rather than assume it matches the lab. For a manual delivery and replay, create a fresh directory:

This output was observed for the first delivery in the captured run. Identical replay also completed; test-only audit triggers recorded zero additional catalog writes. Merely seeing two catalog rows would not prove that: an upsert could rewrite the same rows without increasing their count.

The ack field is a printed illustration of where acknowledgment would occur. It does not acknowledge a message to a real broker.

The imports table stores the caller's import ID, the original file bytes, their SHA-256 hash and the expected row count. Acceptance commits separately before processing begins, so an accepted import can exist with no completed rows.

For the supplied file, the captured record is:

The ID belongs to one exact delivery payload. Reuse it for a redelivery of those bytes. A corrected file needs a distinct ID; changing even whitespace under the existing ID is rejected by the code. The altered-input test changes a price from 1299 to 1300 cents, confirms a nonzero exit containing different bytes, and checks that prior records are unchanged.

Validation happens before acceptance. The payload must be a nonempty array; each row must have exactly sku, name and price_cents. Names and SKUs must contain non-whitespace text, prices must be nonnegative integers, and the file cannot contain duplicate SKUs. This makes row position a usable work identity within this immutable file. It is not a general identity for a product across future imports.

The stored bytes are immutable by application contract. This code does not prevent an administrator from directly altering the database.

Each row is identified by (import_id, row_number), enforced as the primary key of completed_rows. The worker starts BEGIN IMMEDIATE before checking whether that row is complete.

If a result already exists, it skips the catalog write. Otherwise, it upserts the product and inserts the completed-row record, including the resulting SKU, name and price, within that transaction. Commit makes both changes visible together. The exception handler rolls back before propagating an ordinary failure; the full code below preserves that handler and the replay check.

This implementation uses SQLite's single-writer behavior for coordination. SQLite's transaction documentation explains that BEGIN IMMEDIATE starts a write transaction immediately and can fail if another writer is active. The connection waits up to 15 seconds for a lock. That is bounded waiting, not unlimited recovery or a throughput claim.

In the duplicate-worker test, two fresh worker processes target the same import and local database. A third connection holds a write transaction while the test checks that both workers are still running. After releasing it, both workers complete. Audit triggers count exactly two catalog writes for the two input rows.

That observation is narrower than claiming the workers can run all their writes in parallel: SQLite serializes them. Longer contention can still fail.

The importer counts completed rows and compares that count with the accepted row count. It prints complete only when those counts agree. There is no independent success flag that can get ahead of row processing.

The captured catalog contains SUP-101, Steel bottle, at 1299 cents and SUP-202, Canvas bag, at 850 cents. Each has a completed-row result with the corresponding values. Support can inspect the records without relying on a process that may have disappeared:

The completed result describes what that import committed. A later import with a different ID can update the same SKU, so an older result is not proof of the catalog's current value. This lab does not solve ordering between different imports or prevent an older delivery under a different ID from overwriting newer data.

The tests launch real Python subprocesses and use os._exit at two explicit failure points. Each retry runs in a fresh process against the same temporary database. These are abrupt process exits, not operating-system crashes or power-loss tests.

Before the first row commits, the process exits with code 71. The accepted import remains, but the catalog and completed-row tables both contain zero rows. A fresh retry completes both rows. Support's next action follows from that saved state: resume the accepted import using the same ID and bytes.

After the first row commits, the process exits with code 72 before printing the acknowledgment. There is no stdout, but one catalog row and one completed result survive. The retry reaches two completed rows, and an audit trigger observes zero updates to the already committed row. Missing acknowledgment therefore does not mean no work committed.

The suite also checks identical replay, altered-file rejection, and competing workers. Its captured summary is:

Run the supplied suite to exercise these cases safely; it creates isolated temporary databases. The crash flags are test hooks, not operating instructions for valuable data.

The catalog write and result share one local transaction. A remote inventory update cannot join it. If a remote request succeeds and its response is lost, a missing local result does not establish whether repeating that request is safe. That boundary needs the provider's idempotency contract and a reconciliation process, with an owner for unresolved outcomes.

For broader background, Anjana Fernando's Practical Transaction Handling in Microservice Architecture, published November 30, 2020, discusses the move from local to distributed transactions. The local tests here do not validate that broader architecture.

This lab has not tested SQS, PostgreSQL, multiple hosts, network filesystems or machine power failure. synchronous=FULL requests SQLite's commit synchronization; it is not protection against every storage failure. Production ingestion, access controls, migrations and monitoring are omitted. No end-to-end exactly-once guarantee follows from these tests.

A recovery screen built on these records could show the accepted identity, which rows committed, and which remain. A conflicting payload should remain a conflict. An uncertain remote action should remain unresolved. Neither should become a green success badge merely because another worker started.

My guide to background jobs that survive a worker restart develops the broader restart-design questions. The complete local implementation and its tests follow here so this example can be inspected without an external repository.

Save each block under the stated filename. Keep sample.json byte-for-byte if comparing its hash with the captured run, including its final newline. The importer uses the same SQL schema shown in its SCHEMA constant; no separate setup command is needed.

Fractional CTO in Ilford, UK. Co-Founder, CTO and COO at AlphaRages.

#9833. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:

Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:

Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

#9832. How to get found by ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI: the lipp.dev case

Posted on Nov 19 • Edited on Nov 19 • Originally published at lipp.dev • AI-assisted

My site has been live for one day. This is what I did so AI assistants can read it, find it and cite it: every step is in the site's code, and you can check it.

In short. AI assistants that search the web cite pages they can read, that they find in an index (Google's, Bing's or their own) and whose author they can identify. On lipp.dev I worked on those three things: AI crawlers welcomed by name and HTML that reads without JavaScript; Bing, IndexNow and the sitemap; structured data and the same identity everywhere. No tricks: technical SEO done with care.

The new lipp.dev went live on 18 November 2026. I am writing this the day after, so I have no results to show you yet: no charts, no "+300% citations". I'll tell you what I did and why, with links to the official documentation.

The starting point, measured on 19 November: Google had indexed about 38 pages of the site, Bing only 2. I'll measure the results over the coming weeks and update this guide with the real numbers, even if they're disappointing.

When an assistant searches the web to answer you, it reads pages that someone has already discovered and put into an index. There are three main routes:

In practice, a site with solid SEO basics already has a head start. The work "for AI" is mostly: don't block anyone, get indexed beyond Google, and be clear about who you are.

Many sites block AI bots without knowing it, through copied rules or a CDN setting. In my robots.txt I listed them one by one, so the intent is unambiguous:

A useful distinction: GPTBot is for model training, OAI-SearchBot for search. You can block the first, allow the second, and still appear in ChatGPT search. Likewise Google-Extended is about Gemini and doesn't touch Google Search: Google says it affects neither inclusion nor ranking (Google's crawlers). I let them all in: for a freelancer who wants to be known, being read pays off. It's a choice, not a requirement.

lipp.dev is built with Astro, as a static site: every page reaches the browser as complete HTML, with real text and real links (). React only wakes up in the contact form. I can't assume a crawler runs JavaScript, so everything that matters has to be in the HTML.

The site sits behind Cloudflare, which has an option that hides email addresses from spammers: it replaces the address in the HTML and rebuilds it with a script (Cloudflare docs). People see no difference, but anything reading only the HTML finds a placeholder. I turned it off on 19 November: hello@lipp.dev is now in the page source, exactly as people read it. The cost is a bit more spam.

No AI asks for a minimum speed score, but Google lists page experience among the basics that also apply to its AI features. On lipp.dev: static pages on Cloudflare Pages, a single self-hosted typeface, WebP images. In internal tests on 12 November, mobile Lighthouse scored 100 on the home, service and project pages, and on 19 November the server answered in about 0.19 seconds (TTFB).

The sitemap is generated on every build. Every page has its canonical URL and the Italian/English pair declared with hreflang, so no engine mixes up the two versions or takes them for duplicates.

IndexNow is a protocol that lets a site tell search engines a page is new or changed, instead of waiting for them to come by. Bing, Naver, Seznam, Yandex and Yep support it (indexnow.org). On lipp.dev a script runs after every production build, reads the sitemap and submits every URL:

The key is public by design: it sits in a text file on the domain and proves the site is mine. If the call fails, the deploy goes on anyway.

Most people only think of Google Search Console, which of course I set up. But Bing is the base of Copilot and Bing's AI summaries, and since February 2026 Bing Webmaster Tools has a report, still in preview, that shows how often your pages are cited in Copilot and Bing's summaries (Bing's announcement). I verified the domain with a DNS record and submitted the sitemap. For ChatGPT, Bing's weight isn't documented: OpenAI runs its own crawler and doesn't publish how much other indexes count. I cover both routes, since it costs little.

I also submitted the main pages to Brave Search.

llms.txt is a 2024 proposal by Jeremy Howard: a Markdown file at the site root that gives assistants a short, ordered map of the content (llmstxt.org). llms-full.txt isn't part of the proposal: it's a later convention, the long version with all the useful text.

On lipp.dev both are generated on every build from the same data as the pages (services, projects with their results, FAQ), so they can't say anything the site doesn't. I'm cautious about their weight: Google states plainly that its AI features need no such files, and no major engine has confirmed reading them systematically. I keep them because they cost nothing.

Every page of lipp.dev carries a JSON-LD graph with the same core nodes, joined by stable identifiers, so engines understand it is always the same business and the same person:

One rule I always keep: the structured data only says what the page also says.

On 19 November I asked ChatGPT "Who is Lipp?". It described me well, but as an "independent studio": the words of my old site. AI assistants repeat what they find almost word for word. That same day I aligned the title, description, structured data and llms.txt on "freelance web designer and developer".

Then the same sentence and the same details wherever I can be found: Google Business Profile, Bing Places (imported from Google), LinkedIn profile and page, GitHub, Instagram, AddLance, FreelanceDEV. "Luca Piacentini" is a name with plenty of namesakes, and "Lipp" alone is ambiguous: so name, brand and job always travel together.

AI assistants quote concrete sentences: who you are, where you work, what you do, with what results. That's why there is an About page with dates and background, an FAQ with direct answers, and project pages with measured results where there are some.

You can check almost all of it yourself in an afternoon:

In two weeks, and again in two to three months, I'll look at: indexed pages in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools, Bing's AI citations report, and the same questions asked to ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Mode, with date and answer. I'll update the guide on lipp.dev with what I find.

If you have a site, new or in need of fixing, I can do this work for you too: technical audit, robots.txt, structured data, Bing and IndexNow, llms.txt, and the same identity across your site and profiles. I'm a freelancer based in Rome working with businesses all over Italy, and you always talk to me: write to me or see the SEO, GEO & AEO service.

#9828. A Zero Result for Mayastor Is a Scope Finding, Not a Clean Bill of Health

Mayastor is a container-attached storage project for Kubernetes. It exposes a storage management API and is deployed through a control plane that manages volumes and storage resources. A ZoomEye query for title="Mayastor" returned zero matches on November 20, 2026 at 03:40 CST, with sub_type=all, page 1, and pagesize 1.

The zero is a successful query result. It is not a network failure and not proof that no Mayastor deployment exists. The title field may be absent from the API, the management interface may be behind an internal DNS name, or the service may not return a matchable HTML title.

The CNCF OpenEBS self-assessment describes a Mayastor REST API that can perform CRUD-like operations on logical storage resources. It also describes control-plane agents that interact with storage nodes. A storage management API is an administrative surface even when it does not have a polished web page.

An operator who can create, delete, or modify volumes can affect application availability and data durability. A storage API that is reachable from an unexpected network should be reviewed as a control-plane exposure, not as a generic web endpoint.

The OpenEBS Mayastor security documentation states that TLS can serve the REST API over HTTPS on port 8080 and that JWT-based authentication for the REST API is planned. That statement needs to be read in the version actually deployed. It does not establish that every deployment is unauthenticated. It does establish that authentication design is version-sensitive and should be confirmed.

The result supports a narrow claim: no title matched the exact phrase Mayastor in ZoomEye's selected scope at that time. The query used page 1, pagesize 1, and sub_type=all. It did not enumerate every port, certificate, API banner, or custom dashboard.

Do not convert the zero into a statement that Mayastor has no internet exposure. Use it as a reminder to search other fields where appropriate, such as a verified application fingerprint or a distinctive service banner. A product-specific fingerprint must be confirmed before it is treated as valid.

Start from the Kubernetes management cluster. List Mayastor control-plane services, REST endpoints, node agents, and storage classes. Record which endpoints are bound to a pod network, a load balancer, or a host port. Confirm the TLS mode, authentication state, and network policy for each.

Review who can create and modify volume resources, storage pools, and disk resources. Separate storage administration from the workload's service account. A workload should not have broad storage CRUD permissions just because the application team owns the namespace.

Treat the API server, the Kubernetes API, and the data-plane iSCSI or NVMe endpoints as different boundaries. A firewall rule for the management port does not protect the data path. A restrictive Kubernetes NetworkPolicy may not cover a host-network listener.

Monitor control-plane deployment changes, volume creation and deletion, certificate changes, and API access from unexpected sources. A zero public observation can coexist with a healthy internal management plane. The inventory and the network policy are the relevant controls.

If a future query returns matches, compare the product version and endpoint type before interpreting the increase. A new title can reflect a dashboard release or a documentation page. A new API listener may require a different query and a different owner.

The zero result is useful because it forces a precise statement. It does not lower the risk of a misconfigured storage API that is invisible to a title search. Review the real deployment, not only the public count.

#9827. DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:

The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:

The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

Adapted from the original RadixArk article.
