#9824. Building a Browser-Based Image Editor With Web Workers and OffscreenCanvas

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

Photoshop can do everything ScapeStudio does. That is not the point. Preparing photographs for fine art prints and T-shirt production is a specific pipeline: greyscale, curves, threshold knockout with feathered edges, export at 300 DPI across fixed paper and garment sizes. In Photoshop, that is opening each file, running an action, exporting, renaming, repeating. Twenty photographs is an afternoon.

ScapeStudio does those four steps, nothing else, and the entire pixel pipeline runs in a Web Worker. Dragging a curves handle has to re-render the preview in under 16ms or the feel is gone. Main-thread processing on a 24-megapixel shot cannot hit that. A worker with an OffscreenCanvas can.

Canvas 2D is not slow in itself. Every pixel operation on the main thread competes with layout, paint, input handling, and React reconciliation. Luminance conversion on an 8000x6000 image is 48 million pixels, 192 million byte operations. On a warm JIT, around 150ms. For the duration of that loop, the UI is frozen, scrolling halts, and the curves handle stops tracking.

Most web editors work around this by downsampling aggressively and processing the thumbnail, only running the full pipeline on export. That gets interactive curves, but what you see is not what you get. Shadow clipping and highlight roll-off are invisible in a 400-pixel preview.

ScapeStudio processes a 2000-pixel preview in a worker on every parameter change, and runs the full-resolution pipeline only at export. The worker does not block the main thread, so the curves handle drags smoothly while the pipeline works.

The message shape between the main thread and the processing worker is deliberately tight:

Two details are load-bearing. The image moves as an ImageBitmap, not raw ImageData: ImageBitmap is a transferable reference to decoded pixel memory, so postMessage hands the GPU-side resource across thread boundaries without copying. The curves state is pre-baked into a 256-entry Uint8Array lookup table on the main thread before sending. The worker never sees the user's control points; it just indexes the LUT.

This is the serialisation gotcha that kills naive worker pipelines. Send four control point objects and expect the worker to rebuild the spline every frame, and you pay spline evaluation per frame. Send a Uint8Array of 256 bytes, the worker runs one array lookup per pixel, and the spline maths happens once per parameter change, on the main thread, where it is cheap.

A normal is a DOM node. Its 2D context reaches into layout, compositor, and the DOM in ways that only exist on the main thread. You cannot instantiate one in a worker. For years, image processing in workers meant shuttling raw Uint8ClampedArray buffers through postMessage, which either copies (slow) or transfers (you lose the buffer on the sender side).

OffscreenCanvas exists in the Web Worker global scope. Its getContext("2d") behaves like the DOM canvas context and can produce ImageBitmap via transferToImageBitmap. The pipeline is built around that:

Everything after drawImage operates on a single Uint8ClampedArray that never leaves the worker. createImageBitmap returns a transferable bitmap handed back to the main thread by reference. The only bytes that actually cross the worker boundary are the 256-byte LUT in, and a pointer-sized bitmap handle out.

Greyscale uses luminosity weighting, not an RGB average:

Coefficients from Rec. 601 match how the eye perceives brightness. Naive (R + G + B) / 3 loses shadow detail in greens and blows out blues. For fine art prints, weighted luminance is non-negotiable.

Curves is a pre-baked 256-entry LUT applied to the luminance channel:

One array lookup per pixel. No branches, no arithmetic. Fastest possible tonal transformation.

Threshold with feathering modifies the alpha channel based on luminance:

Pixels below lower go fully transparent. Pixels between lower and threshold get a linear alpha ramp. Pixels above threshold are untouched. For t-shirt prep this knocks out studio backdrops while leaving hair and fabric edges soft, rather than the jagged bitmap look of a pure binary threshold.

The obvious way to wire up a Photoshop-style curves tool is Catmull-Rom splines through the user's control points. Mostly works, except when two adjacent points have a steep slope difference: Catmull-Rom overshoots. Drag a shadow point down, the curve dips below zero before recovering. The LUT clamps negatives, so you get a flat black region where you wanted a gentle toe.

ScapeStudio uses monotone cubic Hermite interpolation via the Fritsch-Carlson method, which guarantees no overshoot:

The harmonic mean of slopes plus the radius-3 restriction is what makes it monotonic. The curve still passes through every control point exactly, still feels like Photoshop. It just cannot dip outside the range you drew. 256 evaluations per parameter change, a few microseconds total.

Each pipeline stage reads from the previous stage's output and writes to its own buffer. The source ImageBitmap is never touched. That matters for two reasons.

First, parameter changes only need to rerun from the earliest affected stage. Adjusting feather does not retouch the curves result; it clones the post-curves pixel data and applies threshold to the copy. After curves run, the print output is captured, then a fresh Uint8ClampedArray is allocated and thresholded independently for the t-shirt preview.

Second, the original image is still available at full resolution for export. The preview pipeline works on a downsampled 2000-pixel version for interactive feel; the export worker re-ingests the original bitmap, applies the same LUT and threshold values at full resolution, writes PNGs at 300 DPI. Same pipeline, different sampling.

The main-thread glue is deliberately thin but does one thing that matters: it debounces worker dispatch by 100ms:

Without this, dragging a slider fires dozens of worker dispatches per second. The worker processes one at a time, a queue builds, the preview falls behind. 100ms is long enough to coalesce a drag gesture, short enough that the output feels live.

One worker instance is reused across the session. Worker startup costs a few hundred milliseconds; you only pay it once.

The export worker is the same pipeline at full resolution, looped over configured sizes, written into a zip client-side:

Each size gets a fresh OffscreenCanvas at target pixel dimensions (cm at 300 DPI), the cropped source draws into it, the pipeline runs, convertToBlob produces a PNG. The t-shirt output clones the buffer, thresholds, exports separately. All blobs go into a JSZip folder and save as one archive. No server round trip. A 20-photograph batch at six sizes produces 240 PNGs and never leaves the browser.

The interactive budget is 16.6ms per frame. The worker pipeline on a 2000-pixel preview takes 30-50ms depending on image and device. Over budget for a single frame, which is why the main thread never waits on it. The drag gesture updates React state at 60fps from input events; the worker processes the latest coalesced state on its own clock; the result paints when it arrives. The preview trails the drag by one or two frames, the UI never stutters.

Moving the pipeline off the main thread is not an optimisation. It is the architectural choice that makes everything else possible. Once pixel loops live in a worker, the main thread only schedules messages and paints bitmaps. The curves handle stays under your cursor. The tab does not beachball on a 24-megapixel shot.

Purpose-built beats general-purpose. Four things, in a worker. Enough.

#9823. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

Jasper is a content writing and content generation tool that uses artificial intelligence to identify the best words and sentences for your writing style and medium in the most efficient, quick, and accessible way.

Key Features

  • Blog posts have been optimized for search engines and rank high on Google and other search engines. This is a huge plus for online businesses that want to generate traffic to their website through content marketing.

The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Key Features

  • Identifies  top three interests based on metrics like time on page, recency, and frequency of each contact
  • Works with every ESP and CRM

3. Seventh Sense

  Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers 

Key Features 

  • AI determines the best send-time and email frequency for each contact
  • Connects with HubSpot and Marketo

4. Phrasee

  Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

Key Features 

  • Instantly generates millions of human-sounding, brand-compliant copy variants
  • Creates tailored language models for every customer
  • Learns what your audience responds to and rebuilds the prediction model every time

HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

  • Provides suggestions for your topic clusters and related subjects

It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Key Features

  Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Key features:

  • Finds gaps and opportunities for new content creation, prioritized by their probable impact and your chance of ranking

The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Key features:

  • Makes it easy for shoppers to filter reviews and find the exact information they’re looking for
  • Analyzes customer feedback and sentiments to help you improve your products
  • Integrates with most leading eCommerce platforms, including BigCommerce, Magento, and Shopify.

11. Albert AI

  Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

  Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

Key features:

  • Breaks down large amounts of data to help you customize campaigns
  • Plugs into your marketing technology stack and can be used across diverse media outlets, including email, content, paid media, and mobile

Final Saying

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. #9822. Extracting roof measurements from PDFs with LLMs, and why the model is the smallest part

Posted on Nov 19 • Originally published at mahmadmanzoor.com

A roofing distributor cannot price a tile roof without numbers: total area, the area at each pitch, and the lengths of every ridge, hip, rake, eave and valley. Those numbers already exist. They sit inside PDF reports from EagleView, RoofScope, Hover, Roofr and a few others, each with its own layout, units and quirks. Before we built DocScan for the Brava Roof Tile Pro Portal, someone re-typed them into a quote form by hand.

It sounds like a weekend job: send the PDF to a model, ask for JSON, fill in the form. It is not. Below is why that version breaks on real uploads and what we shipped instead. The prompt turned out to be the smallest part.

The first prototype was exactly that: one PDF, one prompt, one JSON object. It worked on the demo report and fell over inside a week of real uploads. Each failure was specific, and each one became a test.

One number, two readings. Only one is a roof.

Units. Reports label area in "SQ" (a roofing square is 100 sq ft) or in square feet. A model that reads 32.4 SQ as 32.4 sq ft gives you a roof one hundredth of its real size. A dropped decimal does the opposite. Nothing about the JSON looks wrong.

Double counting. RoofScope reports have a "Project Totals" table grouped by slope category (Flat, Low, Standard, Steep) and a separate "Totals (SQ)" table by actual pitch. Read both and you count the roof twice. Hover repeats the same geometry on several pages.

Pitch notation. Some tables write "6" in the header and mean 6/12. Some write 16:12. A model will happily normalise one of them and drop the other.

Empty answers. Reasoning models can spend their whole output budget thinking and return nothing at all. That is not an exception you can catch; it is a successful response with no text in it.

One confidence number. Ask a model how confident it is and it returns 0.92 for the whole document, which tells a reviewer nothing about which field to check.

The advanced pipeline. Green stages are where most of the accuracy comes from.

The advanced pipeline is a sequence of small stages. Each one writes its name and a progress number to the job row, so the UI can poll and support can see exactly where a job stopped.

Most vendor reports have a real text layer. PyMuPDF can read it in milliseconds, and the vendor is obvious from a handful of markers in that text. When the local fingerprint matches we know the vendor and the page numbers of the length diagram, the pitch diagram and the measurement table, with confidence 0.99 and no model call. The AI discovery step only runs when that fails.

EagleView goes further. Its reports carry vector geometry, so we parse the measurements locally from text and strokes. Those values are deterministic and are marked as read directly from the report. The model only fills the gaps.

That cuts cost and raises accuracy at the same time. The best LLM call is the one you never make.

Only the pages that matter reach the model.

Counting intersections (where an eave meets a hip, a hip meets a ridge) is a vision task. We render at most four pages: the length diagram, the pitch diagram and the measurement table, at 2x zoom. The prompt names the legend explicitly and tells the model to ignore the colour swatches, count each junction once, and not to count the same geometry from two different pages. Any count we could compute locally overwrites the model's.

A roof report contains redundancy. The per-pitch areas must add up to the total area. That gives you a free validator that needs no second model:

If the numbers only agree after dividing by 100, the unit label was wrong. If they do not agree at all, the job is flagged for review.

RoofScope gets a second, narrow model pass that reads only the "Totals (SQ)" table, and that correction is accepted only when its rows sum back to the total within 10 sq ft. Otherwise we keep the earlier data and flag it.

The per-pitch areas have to add up to the total.

The JSON schema asks for a confidence score and a short reason for every field, and the prompt says so plainly: score each field on its own, use 0 when a value is missing, do not copy the document score everywhere. Then the server ignores half of what the model said.

The score is a product of where the value came from and what the model said about it.

The reason text the user sees is generated from the final score, not taken from the model, so the label can never disagree with the number. A value read by the local parser says "Read directly from the EagleView report." A value at or under 0.9 says "Estimated from related measurements in the roof report."

The OpenAI SDK's built-in retries are switched off (max_retries=0). When a stage fails, it is retried once on the other vendor: OpenAI to Gemini, or the reverse, using the same JSON schema converted to Gemini's format. The job records which provider and which model actually answered.

Two lessons from running this on AWS Fargate with Gemini through Vertex AI. First, Vertex rejects a Content object with no explicit role="user", which the public Gemini API accepts, so code that worked locally failed in production. Second, check whether the fallback can authenticate, not whether an API key variable exists. We moved Gemini to workload identity federation, and a check for GEMINI_API_KEY would have silently disabled the fallback the day that key was retired.

A failed job never ends on an empty screen.

For a sales tool, a failed job is worse than a wrong one. A wrong value in an editable form costs a reviewer ten seconds. A failed job means the report is re-typed from scratch.

So the pipeline has three levels. The full run. If any stage throws, an editable fallback that keeps whatever evidence exists. If that throws too, a forced result with deliberately ugly defaults (area 0, pitch 0/12) so a reviewer cannot miss them.

Every path ends on the same screen: the original report on the left, editable fields on the right, a confidence badge and reason on each field, and a button that sends the file to Brava's team in a support chat if the user wants a human to check it.

The Pro Portal quotes view, where extracted reports turn into quotes.

Nothing here is clever. It is the checking and the fallbacks that make it safe to hand a model's numbers to someone who is about to quote a real roof.

Do not send the whole PDF to a model and ask for JSON. DocScan, built for the Brava Roof Tile Pro Portal, fingerprints the vendor locally, parses text and vector geometry where it can, and uses a model only to fill gaps. It sends at most four rendered pages to a vision model, then validates the numbers against the document.

Find redundancy in the document and use it as a check. A roof report's per-pitch areas must add up to the total area. If they only agree after dividing by 100, the unit label was wrong and the value is repaired. If they do not agree at all, the job is flagged for review.

Units and double counting are the usual causes. Reports label area in SQ (100 sq ft) or square feet, so reading 32.4 SQ as 32.4 sq ft shrinks the roof a hundredfold. RoofScope also has two totals tables, and reading both counts the roof twice. The JSON looks fine either way.

Not as given. Asked for confidence, a model returns something like 0.92 for the whole document, which tells a reviewer nothing. DocScan asks for a score and a short reason per field, then recomputes confidence on the server from where each value came from, such as the local parser, and what the model said.

The user should always land on something they can edit. DocScan has three levels: the full run, an editable fallback that keeps whatever evidence exists, and a forced result with deliberately ugly defaults like area 0 and pitch 0/12. A wrong value in an editable form costs ten seconds, while a failed job means re-typing.

Originally published on my site. More posts and projects at mahmadmanzoor.com.

#9818. How many people does a business application take? The redb ecosystem and a short answer

Posted on Nov 19 • Originally published at redbase.app

Half of a team writes not the business but everything around it. How **redb **takes that half off your hands, and why with it an analyst with AI can build an integration.

How many people on your team write the wrapping around the business? The broker connection, the database migration, the zero-downtime deployment, the dashboard, the login. It has to be done, it costs money, and it is the same everywhere. You pay for that work again in every project, and now you pay for it in tokens too: the AI writes the same plumbing, gets it wrong and rewrites it on your bill.

redb has already written that part. It is an open .NET ecosystem: data storage, an integration engine, a host for modules and a login server. This article is about how many people and how much AI work are left when everything around the business is already there.

Data is a class. You write a plain C# class, put an attribute on it, and redb stores it in PostgreSQL, SQL Server or SQLite:

A process is a route. For example: pick up XML files from a folder, check them against a schema and send them to Kafka. A good file moves to done, a bad one to error, where a person can look at it:

An external system is an address string. file://, kafka://, sftp://, soap://, as4://: redb.Route has 30 transport packages and 53 address schemes, from brokers and databases to mail, SOAP and European document exchange. To connect to a system, you name its connector.

Tables and migrations. A new entity usually starts with a meeting: which tables, which relations, which indexes, who writes the migration. Here an entity is a class. Foreign keys, indexes and uniqueness are already in place, and the schema follows the class at startup. The limit: a field removed from the class is removed from the database by default. When an old and a new version of the application run side by side, you turn that mode off.

One example shows it best. The business says: "Let's keep an employee's skills, several of them." In a usual schema that is a fork. Either a separate table: a migration, a foreign key, an index, a join in every query, mapping code. Or a JSON string: cheap today, awkward to search by element, and redone at the next change of requirements. Even with AI that is hours: the model writes either option, but choosing, checking and later redoing it is people's work.

In redb it is one line in the class above, public string[]? Skills. You can search right away:

Each skill is stored as its own row with a foreign key to the employee. The developer describes what an employee is, and the system decides how to lay it out in tables. That is why the business can afford to experiment: a new field is one more property of a class.

Speed. The usual question: isn't this slower than "normal tables"? We checked on the same employee model, which a usual schema spreads over 41 tables. We took the 98 tasks EF Core can do without raw SQL and timed one run of each: redb Pro on PostgreSQL took 189 ms on average, EF Core 703 ms. EF Core is faster where data is flat or where there are many small saves of one object each. If that is your profile, use EF Core. Every example with its time and query count is on the results page, and anyone can repeat the run.

Integrations. A broker connection with retries, dead letters and deduplication usually takes a week to write and a month to fix. Here it is an address string plus ready integration patterns: retry, content-based routing, aggregation, idempotent intake. A transaction in a route is one word: first the database commits, then the sends to brokers go out, then the incoming message is acknowledged, always in that order. The limit: it is not a distributed transaction. HTTP, mail and files run at once, and processes that last hours need a pattern of their own.

Deployment and operations. Routes live as modules in the redb.Tsak host. You drop a new module into a folder, and the host picks it up without stopping the other modules or losing messages in flight. The dashboard, metrics, OpenTelemetry traces and the log are already there. A message a route sent to the host's dead letter queue is replayed or discarded by an operator from the console, with no developer woken up for it. There is a cluster with leader election and signed images. The limit: the server, the OS, TLS and database backups are still your administrator's job, there is just less of it.

Login. redb.Identity is an OAuth 2.1 and OpenID Connect server that installs as a package. We run it against the OpenID Foundation's official test suite: no module fails in the Basic OP and Config OP plans. Three modules need a person to take a screenshot in the browser; they last passed by hand in July. We don't carry the OpenID Certified mark, which is a separate paid procedure.

Document exchange with Europe. If your partner in the EU requires AS4 (e-invoicing, customs, energy, the public sector), the usual answer is a separate Java server next to the application. Here it is a connector. In November its version 4.6.1 passed the European Commission's conformance testing: eDelivery AS4 Profile 1.16, Common Profile, 76 of 76 required tests. The Commission has put redb.Route.As4 on its list of conformant products.

The limit: the certificate is for 4.6.1, later versions have not been through the tests again. It covers the eDelivery common profile. Peppol has a profile of its own, and we have not been tested against it.

With the redb libraries, an analyst with AI can run an integration project.

Here is how it works. The analyst knows the process: where an order comes from, what to do with it, where to send it. The AI knows the markup. The ecosystem knows the technology. The analyst states the task in words, the AI builds an XML route from ready connectors and patterns, and then the checks take over.

Every project created from a template already has an AGENTS.md file with rules for GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Codex and Claude Code: elements only from the schema, secrets only as configuration keys. The markup schema is generated from the real packages. If the model still makes up an element or an option, the package check refuses it before deployment: it names the file, line and column, and answers a typo with "'perod' is not an option of the Timer endpoint. Did you mean 'period'?". The VS Code extension completes from the schema and draws the route as a graph: the analyst looks at the picture and sees whether the process is built right.

The analyst checks what the process means; the machine checks the syntax. That is where the savings come from. Fewer people in the chain: no developer translating the analyst's words into code and then explaining why it came out wrong. And a shorter loop of "the AI wrote it, it failed, the AI rewrote it": the check catches the error before it reaches a server. We have not measured how many tokens this saves.

The limit: an analyst with AI builds routes from what is there. That is connectors, integration patterns, calls to your services, redb objects. Your own code with business calculations is written in C#, and that is a developer's work. A connector that is not on the list is C# work too. The developer stays on the team and no longer writes the plumbing.

In money, nothing. The core, the integration engine, the host and the login server are open source under Apache 2.0. The Pro packages are closed but free: no key, no limits, commercial use included. Everything runs inside your perimeter, the data stays in your database, and nothing goes out. The open part lives in four public repositories, tests included.

Releases come often: eight weeks from 4.0 to 4.7. There is no long-term support branch, but the 4.7.x line gets fixes for critical defects and fixes on request. It is the last line on .NET 8 and 9: Microsoft ended their support on 10 November, and from 4.8.0 on the packages target .NET 10 and 11 only. And somebody has to run the host: ordinary administrator work.

One redb-tsak-stack container brings up the host and the dashboard on SQLite, with no external database and no key. One template creates a route project:

There are 21 route templates: files, Kafka, RabbitMQ, mail, REST, AS2, AS4, redb storage and more. The module goes into the modules/ folder, the host picks it up, and the route shows up on the dashboard.

Not a migration. A pilot: one module, one integration that hurts you today. Take a process a developer looks after now, give it to an analyst with AI, and see how many people and how much time it takes. If it doesn't fit, you lose a day.

Code and documentation: github.com/redbase-app. More on what the ecosystem replaces and what it costs in the article for those choosing a platform.

Which integration would you hand to an analyst first? Tell us in the comments.

#9817. I Sent 12 AI Shoppers Through a Broken Checkout, but Only One Bought Anything

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

Three telescopes, $101.96 each, plus $26.97 shipping. The cart wanted $128.93.

I was running release 2.1.3 of the OpenTelemetry Demo. Its frontend added each product's price once, regardless of quantity. The right total was $332.85. There's an upstream report of this in issue 1526. I kept 3.1.0 as a separate clean reference.

A checkout script could still place the order. I wanted to see if a browser agent would check the cart total before paying.

I built Walkout with a purchase goal and a short persona card for each shopper. Playwright returns a browser observation, the model chooses an action, and the runner carries it out. Then it sends back the next observation with the earlier steps.

Muse Spark 1.3 runs that loop. It can click, select, type, press a key, scroll, or give up. The shop has to show an order confirmation before I count a purchase, even if the model says it's done.

For the recording, I told the shoppers to buy three telescopes and check the quantity, price, shipping, and total. If the arithmetic didn’t agree, they were supposed to leave. The counts below show how the agents did on that task.

The profiles needed different browser conditions or I would just have twelve copies of the same test. Rosa gets a budget phone profile with slower CPU and network settings. Margaret has enlarged text, Lucía an es-MX locale. Dev uses keys. Amara gets the accessibility tree.

Dev sees a plain screenshot and can use keyboard actions. Giving him numbered targets he could click would let him get around a focus problem without ever seeing it. Amara's tree references give her a different view of the page again.

I can repeat those configurations. They don't reproduce every phone or a person's full screen reader session, and the recordings let me see exactly which inputs each simulated shopper had.

One shopper bought before the patch. Eleven left, and ten cited the quantity calculation. I saved each shopper’s explanation next to the browser steps that led to it.

Lucía explained in Spanish that the total charged for one telescope plus shipping. In her replay I can see what the browser showed her before she gave up.

An early smoke run got stuck scrolling between the total and the checkout form for twelve steps. The shopper had already read the cart. I wasn't returning its notes with the history, though, so that useful observation kept dropping out of the next decision. Passing the notes back fixed the loop.

The native quantity dropdown caused another problem. Its open menu didn't appear in the headless screenshot. Repeated taps weren't going to make that screenshot any more informative. I added a select action so the shopper could choose the quantity.

Those were my bugs. Having the saved steps helped me find them before blaming the storefront.

The October 28 model ledger has 1,862 calls. They added up to $8.33742325, or $8.34. I tracked model calls, so the figure leaves out server costs and my time.

The November 4 takes and work added $6.11. By the end of that recording I’d spent $14.45 on model calls across the project.

Spark reads the saved reasons for leaving and picks source files. Muse Wonder 1.0 proposes replacements, and another Wonder call reviews them.

The change was in CartItems.tsx. It multiplied by quantity in the whole-unit sum and in the nanos sum. The existing carry from nanos into units stayed in place.

Another call to the same model approved the patch. Release 2.1.3’s frontend had no test command. Its image build runs type checking and lint, and Walkout won’t serve a patch if that build fails. A successful build still couldn’t tell me what three telescopes cost.

The rebuilt frontend replaced the release image on the same port. I emptied the cart, added three telescopes and checked the total before ordering. Then I sent the same twelve profiles through it again.

Nine bought this time. Rosa couldn't open the full cart on her phone profile. Dev couldn't reach the quantity or Add To Cart controls with the keyboard. Lucía checked the peso arithmetic and found a one-cent difference.

I left Rosa, Dev and Lucía red on the board so I could find the purchase attempts that still needed work. The profiles stayed the same across the two rounds. Their model-chosen actions can vary from one run to the next.

The current repo has browser checks for the original, clean and patched shops. They check the three-telescope total without a model API. The November 11 run has its own saved results and spend ledger. The screenshots and results above are from November 4.

I Put a 42-Desk Design Studio Inside My Coding Agent

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

#9814. Taphonomy 0.2.0: exFAT recovery, labelled UNVERIFIED on purpose

Taphonomy is my deleted-file recovery tool for disk images, written in Rust: https://github.com/fahadbilalsaleem/taphonomy

v0.1.0 recovered from FAT32. v0.2.0 adds exFAT, the filesystem on most SDXC cards and many large USB drives.

On FAT32, deleting a file erases its cluster chain, so a recovery has to assume the file was contiguous. exFAT is kinder: after a deletion, the entry set, the cluster chain and the data usually survive. So Taphonomy reads the extent the metadata states instead of assuming one.

It still recovers only when every condition holds:

the entry set’s checksum is valid; the allocation is well formed; every cluster is free in the allocation bitmap; no other claim the walk saw shares a cluster; with --recover, the content is not zeros only.

Anything else is refused, and the report names the condition that refused it. The bitmap itself is believed only once it agrees with every live file and structure the walk found. And recovery runs in two phases: the walk records every deleted entry set first, and only then decides each one, so a claim found later in the walk can still refuse an earlier set.

Why every exFAT recovery is labelled UNVERIFIED

Metadata can pass every check while the clusters under it hold stale data that is not zeros. So each recovered file is labelled UNVERIFIED, with the checks it passed, and never a claim that the data is the file’s. A matching digest doesn’t raise the label either: the label says how the bytes were found, and a comparison is reported separately.

The rules were measured before they were coded

Before writing the code, I tested the rules against ground truth that no tool under test produced: NIST’s twenty exFAT deleted-file-recovery images (made on macOS, every block tagged), images Windows made, and one Linux made. Three findings changed the rules first:

On NIST’s dfr-13, the rule as written recovered a file whose cluster held another file’s later append. Corrected before any code. A stricter rule (any unseen claim refuses every set on the volume) recovered nothing on all twenty images, because every one holds a deleted directory. Withdrawn. Leaving deleted directories unread let five of macOS’s own files be recovered over data written by a file inside one. Deleted directories are now read for their claims, although nothing inside them is recovered yet. Results

On NIST’s eleven MBR exFAT images plus the Linux-made one:

Deleted sets decided 687 Agreeing with checker scripts written separately from the code 687 Files recovered 630 Correct against ground truth 630

Every part of that check was shown able to fail before I relied on it: a changed byte, another file’s content under a set’s name, and a refused set reported as recovered each produced a failure.

Two wrong recoveries remain under every rule I measured. On NIST’s dfr-02 and dfr-05, a macOS ._501 file is recovered holding stale fseventsd data. No metadata check can tell stale, non-zero data from the file’s own. Both are GPT images, which Taphonomy doesn’t read yet, so 630 of 630 is not evidence they’re fixed. That is exactly what the UNVERIFIED label is for.

Limitations: disk images only, MBR with 512-byte sectors (no GPT yet); FAT12 and FAT16 identified but not read; NTFS unsupported; nothing inside a deleted exFAT directory is recovered; FAT32 names are 8.3 only. 22 decision records, 650 tests, GPL-3.0.

Would you rather a recovery tool refuse more, or recover more and label it honestly?

#9811. Microsoft's Python Agent Framework Hijack: What Package Compromise Teaches About Agent Supply Chain Security

Posted on Nov 19 • Originally published at mech.app

Microsoft's agent-framework package on PyPI was compromised to distribute info-stealing malware through versions 1.26.1 and later. The attack vector appears to be unauthorized access to an administrator account on Microsoft's GitHub organization, which allowed attackers to push malicious releases to the official package repository.

This is not a typosquatting attack or a dependency confusion exploit. This is a direct compromise of the upstream source, which means every standard supply chain defense (lock files, hash verification, SBOM generation) fails if you trust the publisher identity without verifying the artifact contents.

Agent frameworks sit at a privileged position in the execution stack. They orchestrate tool calls, manage state, handle credentials, and often run with elevated permissions to interact with external APIs, databases, and file systems.

When you install an agent framework, you are granting it:

A compromised framework can exfiltrate credentials during initialization, inject backdoors into agent execution loops, or modify tool call responses to manipulate downstream logic.

The attack chain probably looked like this:

The malware likely executes during package installation (via setup.py or __init__.py) or at framework initialization, before any agent logic runs.

Most Python projects use pip with requirements.txt or pyproject.toml. Standard practices include:

None of these defenses help if the attacker controls the publisher account and can push new versions with valid signatures.

The most practical short-term defense is artifact hash pinning with manual verification during updates. This means:

This does not scale well for large dependency graphs, but it works for critical framework dependencies like agent orchestrators.

Agent frameworks should run in isolated environments with minimal privileges. The compromise surface depends on deployment shape:

Monolithic deployment (agent framework and business logic in the same process):

Sidecar deployment (agent framework in a sidecar container):

Serverless deployment (agent framework in a Lambda or Cloud Run function):

Kubernetes operator deployment (agent framework as a cluster operator):

The worst-case scenario is running an agent framework with cluster-admin privileges in a Kubernetes environment. The malware could deploy cryptominers, exfiltrate secrets from all namespaces, or establish persistent backdoors.

Even with perfect dependency verification, runtime monitoring provides a second line of defense. Indicators of compromise in an agent framework include:

This approach logs all environment variable access and network calls during framework initialization. Anomalies trigger alerts in your observability platform (Datadog, Honeycomb, Grafana).

Agent deployment pipelines should enforce verification gates before promoting packages to production:

This pipeline blocks deployment if vulnerability scans fail or if package hashes do not match pinned values.

Use agent frameworks from major vendors (Microsoft, LangChain, CrewAI) if you need rapid prototyping and can tolerate supply chain risk with compensating controls. Pin exact versions with hashes, run in isolated environments, and monitor runtime behavior.

Avoid agent frameworks in production if you cannot implement artifact verification, runtime monitoring, and network isolation. Build your own lightweight orchestration layer using standard libraries (asyncio, httpx, pydantic) and explicit tool call routing. The additional engineering cost is justified when the blast radius of a compromise includes customer data or production infrastructure.

Never run agent frameworks with elevated privileges (cluster-admin, root, or AWS admin roles). Use least-privilege IAM roles, ephemeral credentials, and separate execution contexts for each agent instance.

The Microsoft incident proves that publisher identity is not sufficient for trust. Verify artifacts, isolate execution, and monitor behavior.

#9809. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

#9807. Why No Man's Sky Bet on a Custom Engine: The Procedural Math Behind 18 Quintillion Planets

No Man's Sky runs on a proprietary internal engine built by Hello Games for deterministic procedural generation — not Unity, not Unreal. That choice explains both the 2016 disaster and the decade-long comeback: over 18 quintillion planets from a single 64-bit seed, almost nothing stored on servers, and a tiny Guildford team still patching the same tech into Light No Fire today.

The short version: Hello Games rented attention from Sony but refused to rent technology. A licensed engine in 2013 could not promise 18 quintillion consistent planets on PS4. Their own math could — at the cost of having to invent multiplayer, base-building, VR, and cross-play on top of it later, in public.

Hello Games was founded in February 2008 by Sean Murray, Grant Duncan, Ryan Doyle and David Ream in Guildford, and No Man's Sky was developed by only a small four-person team led by Murray before its VGX 2013 reveal, with Sony Interactive Entertainment handling promotional and publishing help for PS4 Hello Games history.

It launched worldwide for PlayStation 4 and Windows in August 2016 — NA August 9, EU August 10, PC August 12 — then Xbox One in July 2018, PS5 and Xbox Series X/S in November 2020, Switch in October 2022, macOS in June 2023, Switch 2 in June 2025, and iOS on October 28-29, 2026 release history.

The defining technical claim has never changed: nearly all stars, planets, flora, fauna and encounters are created through deterministic algorithms and random number generators from a single seed, with that 64-bit value leading to over 18 quintillion planets to explore how the universe is generated. Very little data is stored on servers — elements are recalculated when you approach them, so other players see the same planet if they travel to the same coordinates server model.

Ten years later, the scale is still absurd: as of August 2026, Murray said players had visited less than 1% of the planets in the game tenth anniversary note.

Light No Fire, announced at The Game Awards 2023 and in development since 2018, uses the same internal engine as No Man's Sky, and optimizations made for it enabled Hello Games to port No Man's Sky to iOS by October 2026 shared engine. Hello Games describes itself simply as a small studio that likes to harness technology to make creative, ambitious games studio statement.

That last line is the tell. This was never an Unreal shop that pivoted. It is a technology-first shop that kept the same hull for a decade.

In 2013 Unity 4 and Unreal Engine 4 could ship beautiful corridors. They could not ship this promise: land on any dot you see, with fauna, flora, trading and combat, on a base PS4 with no loading screen between space and surface.

Three practical reasons pushed Hello Games to go custom:

1. The seed is the server. A licensed engine expects content to exist somewhere — on disk or on a server. No Man's Sky stores almost nothing. Your PS4 recalculates the planet from math. That is why cross-platform play, added in July 2020 cross-play timing, and the 32-player Space Anomaly hub advertised on the official site multiplayer model were possible at all for a 50-person studio — the studio reported 50 employees in 2023 team size. They did not have to pay to host 18 quintillion planets. They only had to host discoveries, bases and sessions.

2. Hiring leverage ran the other way. Most “Why Unreal?” stories are about hiring: rent UE5, hire anyone who knows it. Hello Games did the opposite. With four people at reveal and still tiny years later, a custom engine was a filter. You joined to write planet math, not to wire Blueprints. That kept the team small enough to survive the flood that destroyed much of their hardware on December 24, 2013 flood setback and the launch backlash that followed.

3. The launch wound required an owned engine to heal. No Man's Sky received mixed reviews at launch, with critics praising technical achievement but calling gameplay lackluster, and backlash focused on missing multiplayer and Hello Games going quiet launch reception. Since then Hello Games added multiplayer, base-building, freighters, VR and cross-play through free major updates, now widely cited as one of gaming's greatest redemption stories redemption arc.

My read — and this is analysis, not a Hello Games quote: infinity was customer support. When you cannot handcraft an apology big enough for 2016, you generate it. Every free update — Beyond, Origins, Worlds Part I and II, Voyagers — was cheaper to build because the universe was already math. New biomes, storms and water effects are new functions fed into the same seed pipeline, which is exactly why work on Light No Fire could flow back into No Man's Sky instead of forking.

Procedural generation is creating data algorithmically through human-guided rules plus randomness, used in games to automatically create large amounts of content with smaller file sizes and more variety definition. No Man's Sky is listed there as the extreme case: a game all based upon procedurally generated elements.

The same page warns about “procedural oatmeal” — thousands of bowls that taste the same oatmeal critique.

Here is where I break from the standard critique. Most reviewers treat oatmeal as failure. For No Man's Sky, oatmeal is the menu.

The four pillars are exploration, survival, combat and trading, with mining, scanning, documenting flora/fauna for units, buying and selling, building bases and expanding fleets core loop. None of those verbs requires a hand-authored planet. They require a legible planet: see resource, mine resource, survive hazard, sell, upgrade, leave. Oatmeal is fine when you are hungry for a loop, not a story. The 30+ hours of Atlas story exists, but the retention engine is the commute between dots.

If you want to feel that mining loop in 30 seconds, try Adventure Miner in a browser. You gather ore, haul it to the dock, buy pickaxe power and capacity, and unlock richer islands. It is the same gather-sell-upgrade-push rhythm as the Multi-tool, stripped of planets — which is why it works as a trainer for NMS discipline: capacity before power, routes before grinding.

The <1% visited stat is usually framed as bloat. I read it as insurance. A handcrafted open world depletes. A seeded universe cannot be finished, so it cannot be proven empty. That let Hello Games sell time, not content, while they rebuilt trust update by update.

Starfield, built on Creation Engine 2 and released September 6, 2023 for Windows and Xbox Series X/S (PS5 April 7, 2026), offers more than 1,000 planets, with most landscapes procedurally generated around handcrafted points of interest like New Atlantis Starfield scope. Bethesda heavily modified Creation to add procedural systems.

Outer Wilds does the opposite: a tiny handcrafted planetary system stuck in a 22-minute time loop that resets when the sun goes supernova loop premise.

My take: seamlessness beats fidelity for space fantasy. Starfield tells you space is far by showing you a menu. No Man's Sky tells you space is far by making you fly through colored clouds while your pulse drive spools. That is not a graphics win. It is an engine-architecture win — atmosphere entry, terrain LOD and creature spawning all had to be one continuous system, which a general-purpose engine would have split into levels.

When you want to practice that continuous-flight patience without booting NMS, Build Your Rocket captures the core fantasy in miniature: hold to accelerate, release to coast, climb to reach new planets. NMS is that hold-and-release stretched across galaxies with hazard protection and fuel as the throttle.

Space combat and Sentinel dogfights were thin at launch and still arcade-simple compared to dedicated flight sims. That is the custom-engine tax: Hello Games wrote a universe generator first, a shooter second.

For quick dogfight reflexes — leading targets, breaking off, re-engaging — a browser round of Aces of the Sky: Epic Dogfights is a useful warm-up. Waves of fighters, bombers, helicopters and zeppelin bosses train the same skill NMS space combat actually tests: positioning while tracking multiple projectiles, not complex maneuvers.

Base-building and freighters, by contrast, were cheap to add precisely because the engine is deterministic. A base is just a small list of player edits pinned to seed coordinates. The official site now sells that as the fantasy — from outposts to multi-planet colonies and mobile freighter bases building pitch. The engine did not have to learn persistence. It only had to remember exceptions.

Make the seed do server work. If your world can be recalculated from coordinates, you do not pay to host it. You only pay to host what players change. That is how a 50-person team ships cross-play and VR without a platform-holder backend.

Ship infinity, patch meaning. Launch with systems (mining, scanning, trading, surviving), then add verbs (exocraft, settlements, fishing, corvettes) as functions over the same math. Each update revalues old planets without rebuilding them.

Use ugliness as compression. Early NMS creatures were meme-ugly because the generator combined parts freely. Players forgave it because discovery — naming the beast and uploading it to the Atlas for units discovery economy — paid in social currency. Let players laugh, then let them name the joke.

Do not rent what differentiates you. If your pitch is “every planet different,” your engine must own planet generation. Renting Unreal would have made hiring easier and the game impossible. Hello Games chose the harder hiring path to keep the one feature no license could guarantee.

Plan your second game as engine interest. Light No Fire is described as one Earth-size procedural planet with denser content than NMS planets Light No Fire scope. That is not a sequel. It is the same internal engine pointed at depth instead of breadth — and its optimizations already paid for an “impossible” iOS port. Build tech that funds its own sequel.

My contrarian bet: the next meaningful NMS competitor will not offer more planets. It will offer fewer, denser ones on someone else's engine — and lose the long game, because it will have to handcraft every apology. Hello Games can generate apologies forever.

No Man's Sky bet on a custom engine because only custom math could turn 18 quintillion planets from a marketing line into a shipping build on 2016 hardware, then into a decade of free updates and a second game on the same codebase. The cost was a brutal launch and years of building standard features from scratch. The payoff is a universe that still has 99% left to see — and an engine team small enough to keep going.

If you came here asking “what engine was No Man's Sky made in” — it was not Unity, not Unreal, not Creation. It was Hello Games' own procedural engine, iterated since Joe Danger, hardened by flood, hype and backlash, and now stretched toward an Earth-size fantasy world.

#9804. Go Dispatch Rehearsals Explained — Property Welcome Email Templates and Suppression Lists

Template ownership trades publishing convenience against control over what a queued welcome email will eventually say. TL;DR: for a property management contact form, make the support queue, approved template revision, and suppression decision explicit before handing a message to a delivery adapter; compare transactional email APIs by whether your team can rehearse that decision and recover its evidence. A cheapest-provider claim cannot settle who approves a tenant-facing revision or who handles a suppressed acknowledgment while the support request still needs attention.

The operational rule proposed here is simple: an email decision must never silently become a support-routing decision. A tenant's maintenance request and the acknowledgment of that request have different completion conditions. Treating them as one successful operation makes an attractive dashboard and an unhelpful support system.

Consider a hypothetical production scenario, deliberately bounded to one contact form and one welcome acknowledgment. A new resident submits a maintenance question for property P17; the intended destination is its maintenance queue, while the email welcomes the resident to the support process and explains what happens next. During the queue wait, an editor publishes another template revision. Separately, the recipient becomes suppressed. None of those events should erase the request or move it to a different team.

This is a failure exercise, not a report of an observed outage. Its value is that the expected result can be written down before choosing a provider: preserve the support record, retain the intended queue, and record an explicit email disposition. An acknowledgment that never leaves the application must remain distinguishable from one accepted by a transport, and neither state proves that the maintenance team has handled the request.

The support request exists. Its destination is correct. Its acknowledgment has an explainable disposition. Those are proposed acceptance criteria for this system, not claims about any particular email service. The template owner should approve both the wording and the revision policy: either queued work retains its approved revision, or an explicit migration changes it. Looking up whatever happens to be current at execution time makes that policy accidental.

An editor-friendly interface is only part of template ownership. The useful question is who can approve a change, associate it with a route, reproduce its rendered content, and reverse a mistaken release without guessing which queued requests will change. For this workflow, a support acknowledgment should describe the queue actually selected; copying a leasing template into a maintenance acknowledgment can make correct routing look wrong to the resident.

The cheapest transactional email API is an incomplete selection criterion if its quoted scope leaves template publishing and suppression list operations with your team. Ask who owns those tasks before comparing delivery charges. Don't confuse buying transport with transferring the support workflow's operating responsibility.

For a shortlist containing Amazon SES, Resend, Postmark, and Mailgun, apply the same route-and-template rehearsal to each candidate. Require evidence for revision retrieval, suppression scope, and retry behavior in the configuration being evaluated; a product name alone establishes none of those acceptance results.

The following buy-versus-build comparison describes operating models to evaluate, rather than asserting features of named products. Each row needs a rehearsal using the same sample request before it earns a place in a platform roadmap.

No row wins automatically. If support operations owns wording but engineering owns routing, the split model is a candidate only if both can inspect the same release artifact. Otherwise, the extra handoff can consume more on-call time than it saves in editing effort. Conversely, a small team that already reviews every message change in code may have little reason to introduce a separate publishing system.

The proposed boundary below receives a route snapshot, an approved template snapshot, and a suppression lookup result. It deliberately refuses to turn an unavailable lookup into permission to send. The caller must persist the support request first, then persist this email decision and any resulting work item through a durable application workflow. This function alone provides neither persistence nor concurrency control.

The example identifiers are fictional application data. Revision 3 is a chosen fixture, not a measured production value.

The trap is the interval after this function returns. A ready decision is an input to dispatch, not perpetual permission: the worker needs a current suppression check before each send attempt, and must defer if that check cannot complete. Document the remaining concurrency boundary as well, because a suppression change can race with a transport submission. Pinning content does not freeze recipient eligibility.

For retries, assign a stable application message identity and store the observed attempt state. A timeout can leave acceptance uncertain, so a retry policy needs an explicit reconciliation or duplicate-risk decision; claiming exactly-once delivery from a local status flag would exceed what this example establishes. Keep recipient addresses and rendered tenant details out of routine metric labels.

Use the P17 request as a release fixture and change one condition at a time: substitute a template approved for leasing, make suppression unavailable, mark the recipient blocked, and publish a newer revision while work remains queued. The expected results are rejection, deferral, suppression, and retention of the pinned revision respectively. In every case, verify the stored support request independently. These checks examine the boundary that matters to the resident, rather than whether a template editor can display a preview.

Capacity follows the arrival burst and the backlog, not just a monthly message total. Plan worker concurrency against observed transport latency and permitted request rates; include retries and deferred suppression lookups in the work budget. A recovery drill should establish whether backlog age returns below the team's target without exhausting the downstream allowance. No numerical throughput claim is needed to ask that question.

Track time from durable form acceptance to queue assignment separately from time to acknowledgment disposition. Record submission acceptance and later delivery evidence as separate states where available. A suppressed message should be visible as suppressed, rather than counted as delivered or allowed to poison a retry loop. Alert ownership should follow these boundaries: routing failures belong with the support integration, while rendering and transport failures need their own accountable owner.

Roll out a new template revision with a reviewable render fixture and an explicit promotion decision. For a rollback, specify whether only new requests change or existing queued work is migrated too. That detail affects the work estimate: hosted editing, application rendering, and split publishing each leave some combination of release support, reconciliation, and audit retention with the team. Compare that labor alongside delivery charges, without pretending a volatile unit price explains the whole operating burden.

A synchronous internal notification with no separate editor, no delayed queue, and no welcome sequence may not justify a template promotion pipeline. The durable support record and explicit suppression handling still need a decision, but the revision can be a normal application release artifact. Add machinery in response to a concrete ownership boundary.

For the property contact form, the selection rule is narrower: choose an operating model whose owners can demonstrate the route, reproduce the approved welcome template, and explain the suppression outcome during the same rehearsal. That is a useful comparison even before commercial proposals arrive. The support queue must remain accountable when email cannot proceed.

#9803. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

Find our high-extraction Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour online.

#9799. Your Crypto Exchange's Default Settings Could Change Your Tax Bill

Florida CPA. Crypto accounting and Form 1099-DA reconciliation.

Florida CPA. Crypto accounting and Form 1099-DA reconciliation.

Florida CPA. Crypto accounting and Form 1099-DA reconciliation.

Sell one bitcoin from a balance of two on an exchange, and the confirmation shows a price and a quantity. It does not show which Bitcoin you sold.

That detail decides the tax bill. Take an illustrative investor who bought 1 BTC at $20,000 and another at $90,000, both more than a year ago, then sold 1 BTC at $110,000. If the older coin counts as sold, the gain is $90,000. If the newer one does, it is $20,000. Same trade, same day, a $70,000 difference in reported gain.

For two years the IRS has let U.S. investors settle that question in their own records. That arrangement ends on December 31, 2026. From the first sale of 2027, the choice has to go through the platform holding the coins, which raises a plain question: what can a customer actually tell the platform?

To find out, I read the public tax pages of 15 U.S. crypto platforms between October 27 and 29, 2026. Six of them do not state which coins they sell first.

The rule sits in Treasury Regulation 1.1012-1(j). When a broker holds your coins, and you do not identify specific units by the date and time of the sale, the earliest-acquired units in that account are treated as sold first. That is first-in, first-out, or FIFO, and it runs account by account. Coins at one exchange are not pooled with coins at another.

The IRS granted temporary relief in Notice 2025-7 and extended it in Notice 2026-20. Through December 31, 2026, an investor can identify units on their own books, no later than the date and time of each sale, or record a standing order there before selling. For 2026 sales, the units identified that way control for federal income tax purposes, even if the broker's report shows something else.

After that date, the notice says, taxpayers "may not rely" on the relief. Unless new guidance arrives, the identification has to reach the broker, either as a standing order or as a lot choice on the trade.

A quieter line in the same regulation matters too. When a broker offers only one way to identify units, that method "is treated as a standing order or instruction." The notice switches this off during the relief period for investors using it. From 2027 it applies, so on a single-method platform, the platform's method effectively becomes the customer's own instruction.

I used each platform's own help center, tax pages and terms, read against the IRS rules, and no third-party summaries.

"Not disclosed" means I found no statement on the platform's public pages. It does not mean the platform has no policy. Coinbase, for instance, names FIFO for its institutional Prime accounts but not for retail customers, and Webull's FIFO language covers securities.

Changing the method is a separate question:

Those settings have their own fine print. Kraken's has to be changed from a desktop device and applies only going forward. Coinbase says the method must be chosen before the trade settles, and a new choice covers open and future trades only.

2026 is the first year brokers must report cost basis on Form 1099-DA, and only for "covered" assets: coins bought on that platform on or after January 1, 2026, and kept there. Anything moved in from a wallet or another exchange is noncovered. For people who self-custody, that can be most of what they own.

What happens to those coins depends on where they land:

None of those is your actual cost. The same coin can show up as a blank, a $0 estimate or the price on the day it arrived, depending only on where you sent it.

Robinhood's ordering is no quirk. Treasury Regulation 1.6045-1 tells a broker with no customer instruction and no adequate transfer records to report units it did not acquire for the customer first, and only then work from the earliest date. Your own default is plain FIFO. So the form can list different units from the ones you must treat as sold, and a worked example in Regulation 1.1012-1 shows exactly that.

The form can be right and your return can still need different numbers, with the adjustment shown on Form 8949. That matters because the IRS gets a copy of the form. As attorney and CPA David Klasing explained in a HackerNoon interview on John Doe summonses, the agency has used those orders to spot mismatches between crypto activity and reported taxes. Form 1099-DA puts that data on a standard form for every customer.

Find your method and date it. Look up your platform's default, save the page and note the day you checked. If nothing is published, ask support and keep the written answer.

Identify lots before each 2026 sale, not after. The relief requires the identification no later than the date and time of the sale, so a spreadsheet filled in during January will not rescue December trades. Use something that pins down basis and holding period, such as the purchase date, time and price.

Decide your 2027 setup before your first January sale. If your platform has a setting, pick the method and screenshot it. If it offers lot picking, plan to choose on every order. HIFO is not automatically the better pick: the highest-cost lot may be short-term, and using it first leaves your low-basis coins for a later year. Run both numbers on your own lots.

Export everything now. An earlier HackerNoon piece on crypto tax myths pointed out that most reputable exchanges let you download your transactions into a spreadsheet. Do that for every account, including the ones you rarely open, and keep withdrawals and deposits so both sides of each transfer can be matched.

Add missing basis before forms are generated. The windows are short. Strike asks customers to finish their details before it generates forms in mid-February. Robinhood's cutoff for 2025 sales was January 14, 2026, with a warning that updates after January 7 could delay forms. Assume the next window will be just as tight.

One date to remember: December 31, 2026. It is the last day a lot choice on your own books can count, and Strike warns that its tax year follows UTC, so there the year ends at 7:00 p.m. ET. The next marker follows quickly. Forms are due to customers by February 16, 2027, because February 15 is Washington's Birthday, and those will be the first to carry basis.

The IRS has extended this relief once. Planning on a second extension is a gamble.

Platforms are also still catching up. Several help pages show the old $600 threshold for Form 1099-MISC, although the figure for 2026 is $2,000. So treat any table, this one included, as a snapshot. The full version, with the quote and source link for each platform, is in the study, and the data is archived on Zenodo under a CC BY 4.0 license.

Disclosure: This is general information, not tax advice, DYOR! The author is a Florida CPA who runs a crypto accounting practice.

Florida CPA. Crypto accounting and Form 1099-DA reconciliation.

#9798. An AI sales assistant on Telegram that knows when to hand off

Posted on Nov 19 • Originally published at fhsystems.dev • AI-assisted

Aviago is a tour operator that sells through its own Telegram bot. Its sales team had the problem every chat-based business knows: they were answering the same questions over and over. How much is a flight to this city? Is there anything cheaper? What dates work? Every one of those answers was typed by a person.

So I built an AI sales assistant into the bot. It now answers most of the common questions on its own, in the same tone as Aviago's main sales assistant, and hands the buyer to a person when a person is needed.

This post is how it works, and the design decision that matters most: when the AI stops talking.

The first reply decides a lot. A well-known Harvard Business Review study of 2,241 US companies found that firms that contacted a web lead within an hour were nearly seven times more likely to qualify it than firms that waited even one hour longer.

Chat makes this sharper. On Telegram the buyer is already in a conversation, so they expect a chat-speed answer.

But speed alone is not the goal. A Gartner survey published in August 2026 found that 87% of customers say companies using generative AI for customer service must still give them access to a human. People want the fast answer, and they want to know a real person is there when it matters.

That is the brief for a sales assistant: answer fast, answer correctly, and get out of the way at the right moment.

Aviago's Telegram bot already existed. I didn't replace it. I split the conversation into parts and put the AI between them, so it handles the parts it does well and leaves the rest to people.

The model changed along the way. The first version ran on Groq; it now runs on Claude. Because the workflow is separate from the model, switching was a change in one place, not a rebuild.

The fastest way to lose a buyer's trust is an AI that invents a price. So the assistant doesn't "know" Aviago's prices. It reads them from the same sheet the team updates.

That also means nobody has to retrain the AI when a price changes. The team edits the sheet, as they always did, and the next answer is correct.

Buyers were used to talking to Aviago's main sales assistant. A generic chatbot voice would have felt like a downgrade. So I tuned the assistant to answer the way the team already does: same tone, same kind of phrasing. For the buyer, the conversation feels like the same shop.

How far the assistant goes on its own is not a technical limit. It's a choice the business makes, and it can change.

The assistant hands off when the buyer is ready to book, has a request that needs a person's decision, or simply asks for a person. At that moment the sales team gets the full chat history at once in Discord. Nobody asks the buyer to repeat themselves. A handoff that makes the customer start over is worse than no AI at all.

Most of the common questions are now answered by the assistant, in the team's own tone. The sales team spends its time on buyers who are ready to talk, not on typing the same price again and again.

As Aviago's founder put it: "with his help we added an AI assistant that can work autonomously and hand tasks over to human admins when needed. … Most importantly, we successfully deployed all of these solutions."

If your buyers write to you on Telegram, WhatsApp or Instagram and your team answers the same questions all day, this pattern fits: an assistant that answers from your own data, in your own voice, and hands off to your team at the moment you choose.

I build these as fixed-price projects. Read the Aviago project page, or tell me how your sales chat works today and I'll show you where an assistant would help and where it shouldn't.
