#9794. 5 Real Bugs We Fixed Hardening a Zero-Dependency Node.js MCP Client

While building a zero-dependency Node.js client for the OpenAgentForum Streamable HTTP MCP endpoint (https://openagentforum.com/mcp), five subtle transport and protocol bugs surfaced during code review and live testing.

Here is what broke in practice and how to fix each one cleanly using only built-in node:http / node:https.

Reading an http.IncomingMessage with let data = ""; res.on("data", chunk => { data += chunk; }) calls Buffer.prototype.toString() on each chunk independently. If a 4-byte emoji or Cyrillic character is split across two TCP packets, both halves turn into U+FFFD (``).

Fix: Collect raw Buffer chunks with a hard byte cap, then decode once at end:

`js const chunks = []; let totalBytes = 0;

res.on("data", (chunk) => { totalBytes += chunk.length; if (totalBytes > this.maxBytes) { req.destroy(); return done(new Error(Response exceeded maximum size of ${this.maxBytes} bytes)); } chunks.push(chunk); });

res.on("end", () => { const bodyText = Buffer.concat(chunks).toString("utf8"); // ... }); `

Production Streamable HTTP MCP servers respond with content-type: text/event-stream. A naive /^event:\s*message\s*\ndata:\s*/ regex breaks on \r\n\r\n frame separators, id: lines, multi-line data: blocks, or non-JSON keepalive events.

Fix: Split frames on /\r?\n\r?\n/, join data: lines per frame, skip non-JSON keepalives, and match the JSON-RPC id:

`js for (const ev of parseSseEvents(bodyText)) { let candidate = null; try { candidate = JSON.parse(ev.data); } catch { continue; // skip keepalives or non-JSON comments } if (candidate && candidate.id === reqId) { msg = candidate; break; } } `

Node's timeout option on http.request only fires on socket inactivity. A slow-drip server sending 1 byte per second keeps the socket alive indefinitely. Always pair it with an explicit setTimeout(() => req.destroy(), this.timeoutMs) deadline cleared on completion.

When connecting to untrusted public MCP servers, pin the allowed origin/loopback fixture and enforce an explicit tool allowlist before tools/call, and never echo raw upstream response bodies in thrown error messages.

If you want your AI coding agent to automatically audit and harden MCP clients/servers or write deterministic loopback regression tests, check out my skills on Agensi.

#9792. Data Extraction for AI Agents: 10 MCP Prompts for PDFs, Scans and Forms

Nutrient, formerly is the document layer for agents.

Nutrient, formerly is the document layer for agents.

Nutrient, formerly is the document layer for agents.

Your agent can read an invoice. What it can't do is show you where each number came from, or do the same thing reliably across 10,000 invoices.

Ask Claude Code or Codex to pull the total from a scanned PDF and you usually get one of three things: a guess, a value from the wrong table row, or a confident answer with no way to check where it came from. That's fine for a demo. It isn't fine when the number goes into an accounting system.

This post gives you 10 copy-paste prompts that let an agent read documents properly: pull fields from invoices, tables from statements and text from scans, each value with its source. The agent connects to a data extraction APIover the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Every prompt below was run with the live server connected, and the outputs shown are real.

I tested this on a tilted, noisy scan of a supplier invoice: an image with no text layer at all. Claude read it on its own and got the invoice date and the total right. When I asked where those values were, the best it could do was "top right, about 13% down the page" for the date, and "right side, about 55% down" for the total.

The extraction API returned the same values with evidence:

One caveat: a citation points to the source region, not always the exact word. The date's box is tight and covers the label and the value. The total's box covers the whole totals block, from subtotal to total. A review screen highlights that block, which is still far quicker to check than "about 55% down".

A PDF doesn't store "a table" or "a paragraph". It stores characters at coordinates. Everything a human sees has to be reconstructed: reading order, columns, table cells, which number belongs to which label. Scans are worse, because there's no text at all until OCR runs.

When a general-purpose model reads a PDF directly, four things tend to go wrong:

The fix is to give the agent a document data extraction tool that does the parsing and returns structured output with a source location for every value. The agent keeps doing what it's good at: deciding what to ask for and what to do with the answer.

The server is hosted, so there's nothing to install and no API key in a config file. You sign in once with OAuth.

claude mcp add --transport http --scope user nutrient https://mcp.nutrient.io/mcp

Then start a new session, run /mcp, choose nutrient, and select Authenticate.

codex mcp add nutrient --url https://mcp.nutrient.io/mcp && codex mcp login nutrient

Claude app: Settings → Connectors → add a custom connector with https://mcp.nutrient.io/mcp.

Full setup details are in the MCP server guide.

Each prompt is written the way you'd type it to your agent. Swap in your own file names.

When to use it: any time a number from a document goes into another system.

Extract vendor, invoice number, date, line items and total from invoice.pdf.

What came back: every field correct. Shortened, showing 2 of the 6 line items:

All 6 line items came back, including a −$169.00 credit for returned brackets. The total matches the invoice: $1,835.00 subtotal + $48.00 shipping + $114.91 tax = $1,997.91.

Every value comes with its page, a bounding box and a groundedness score. Here's the citation for the total, as returned:

You don't need to ask for locations; they come back anyway. My first version of this prompt ended with "Show the page and source location for each value." The server turned that into extra fields filled with descriptions like "Upper right, beside 'Invoice date'", which added nothing and caused review flags (see prompt 2).

Two more things to know. The field names are generated for each document: vendor and total here, not a fixed schema. And the output keeps what’s printed: line-item descriptions kept the invoice’s tax marker, as in “Anchor bolt M16 x 200 mm T”.

When to use it: before you import anything automatically.

For every value you extracted, flag anything with low confidence so I can review it before import.

What came back: one value flagged for review: the unit price on the −$169.00 credit line, with a groundedness score of 0.18. The value was correct. Every other field scored between 0.97 and 0.9997 and was marked ready to import.

That's the behavior you want from a review step: it leans towards asking a person. An earlier run, using my first version of prompt 1, came back with 14 flags, mostly on the extra "source location" fields that prompt created. It's a good reason to keep extraction prompts to the fields you need.

When to use it: before chunking documents for retrieval.

Parse report.pdf to Markdown, keeping tables and reading order, and save it as report.md.

What came back: clean headings, the abstract and introduction in order, and the results table intact (as an HTML table, which keeps merged cells). A chart even came back as a table. The test file was a three-page, two-column research paper, and reading order wasn't perfect:

Check the Markdown of a multi-column document before you index it. Single-column documents are much easier.

When to use it: contracts, faxes, anything that arrived as an image.

This is a scanned contract. Parse it with OCR and list the parties, the effective date and who signed.

What came back: the test file was a 3-page image-only scan, slightly tilted and noisy. Parsing took about 13 seconds and cost $0.054 ($0.018 a page). The answer:

Parties: Nexus Digital Solutions, LLC (Service Provider) and Bridgewater Logistics Partners, Inc. (Client)

Signed by: Elena V. Marchetti, Chief Executive Officer, and Derek L. Fontaine, Chief Operating Officer, both dated February 14, 2024

All correct. The noise left stray characters in the parsed text, such as "oo", "ve" and "fe" between two sections, and "Derek L. Fontaine t t" on the signature page. That's normal for scans. The agent's answer stayed clean, and the citations tell you which region to check if something looks off.

When to use it: statements, price lists, reports.

Pull every table from statement.pdf into JSON, then save each table as its own CSV file.

What came back: both tables, the account summary and all 7 transactions, saved as two CSV files. Shortened:

Empty debit and credit cells came back empty, not as zero, which matters if you sum the columns later. The closing balance matched the statement: $7,692.81.

When to use it: an inbox or upload folder with mixed file types.

Classify every file in ./inbox as invoice, receipt, contract or ID document, and move each file into a folder named after its type.

The server classifies; the agent moves the files. Run this one in Claude Code or Codex rather than a chat app.

When to use it: monthly invoice runs, batches of forms.

Extract the same fields from all invoices in ./invoices in one batch, and build one spreadsheet with a row per invoice.

What came back: three invoices from three different suppliers, each with a different layout. The server generated one 20-field schema and applied it to all three. A few columns from the spreadsheet:

All three totals are correct. On the Tidewell invoice, it took the balance due after a $1,500 retainer, not the $6,152.50 in fees.

Tip: run files of one kind together, and say how you want values formatted. Without that, our batch came back with "USD" on two invoices and "$" on the third, and three different date formats. Adding "Use ISO 4217 codes for currency and YYYY-MM-DD for dates" fixed all three. Two things to check after a run like this. A "$" with no country is the model's best guess: here it said USD, citing the supplier's Oregon address. And a field that doesn't fit the format can come back empty: one invoice listed three ship dates, and with the date rule that field came back blank.

When to use it: a new document type you haven't processed before.

Show me which fields you'd extract from claim.pdf before running the extraction.

What came back: 19 proposed fields for a property damage claim form, including claimant_name, policy_number, date_of_loss, type_of_loss and account_number. Each field comes with a rule. Every rule starts with "If no value is observed, return null rather than inventing a value", and then adds specifics. For example, the rule for police_or_fire_report_number is "including an explicit N/A; null if blank". The response said: "Nothing was extracted, billed or stored."

The list isn't fixed. An earlier run on a similar form proposed 21 fields. Edit the list until it has what you need, then use the same list for every file of that type.

When to use it: before sending a document to a vendor, a model, or a colleague who doesn't need the personal data.

Redact names, email addresses, phone numbers and bank account numbers in claim.pdf, then save a redacted copy.

What came back: the claimant's name, email, phone number and account number were removed, both in the form fields and in the free-text description. It also caught the name of a neighbour mentioned in the description. The text is gone from the file, not just covered by a black box. The policy number, address and routing number stayed, because the prompt didn't ask for them.

Two things to watch. The bank name was removed even though the prompt didn't ask for it. And thetyped signature "R. M. Okafor" was removed in one run and left in another. If something must go, name it in the prompt ("…and signatures"), and open the redacted copy before you send it.

When to use it: before you process a folder of documents.

Count the pages in ./invoices and estimate what extracting them will cost at $0.015 per page.

What came back: 3 invoices, 1 page each, so about $0.045. The agent counted the pages itself, locally, without sending anything to the server, so the estimate is free. The rate comes from your prompt. Extraction currently costs $0.015 per page, and parsing $0.009 or $0.018 depending on the mode. To see what you've actually used, check the Nutrient dashboard.

Start with prompt 1 on one real document from your own work, and open the cited regions to check them. Once you trust the output for that document type, move to batches.

The parsing mode decides most of the cost:

Extraction (prompts 1, 5 and 7) ran in understand mode, at $0.015 per page.

Parsing a document to Markdown (prompts 3 and 4) defaults to agentic mode, at $0.018 per page.

On the clean three-page research paper, I reran the parse in understand mode at $0.009 per page. The Markdown was nearly identical, at half the price, in 1.2 seconds.

Agentic mode is for messy scans and complex layouts. For clean digital PDFs, ask for understand mode and compare both on a sample before you process thousands of pages.

Finally, keep a person in the loop for anything that moves money or makes a decision. The citations and confidence scores are there so the review takes seconds, not so you can skip it.

Nutrient, formerly is the document layer for agents.

#9790. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier



 In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

So let’s dive into

1. ChatGPT

ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Pros:

  • Generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts
  • Can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion
  • Can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing
  • Can generate coherent and fluent text, even when completing a given text prompt.

Cons:

  • May generate text that is biased or offensive
  • Can generate text that is not accurate or factually correct
  • May require large amounts of computational resources to run
  • The model can sometimes generate text that is not coherent or fluent, depending on the prompt given.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

2. DALL-E

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Pros:

  • Generates high-resolution images
  • Can generate images from text prompts
  • It can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as generating images of a certain style or category

Cons:

  • May generate images that are not entirely original and could be influenced by the training data
  • May require significant computational resources to run
  • The quality of the generated images may vary depending on the specific prompt

Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is important to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data.

3. Lumen5

Lumen5 is a content creation platform that uses AI to help users create videos, social media posts, and other types of content. It has several features that make it useful for content creation and marketing, including:

Pros:

  • Automatically summarizes text from a blog post, article, or another source into a script for a video or social media post
  • Offers a library of royalty-free videos, images, and music to use in content
  • Has a drag-and-drop interface for easy content creation
  • Can create videos in multiple languages
  • Has a built-in analytics tool to track the performance of created content.

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material
  • The automatic summarization feature may not always capture the main points of the source material
  • The library of videos, images, and music is limited.
  • The analytics feature is basic

Overall, Lumen5 is a useful tool for creating content quickly and easily, it can help automate the process of creating videos, social media posts, and other types of content. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material and it is important to review and edit the content before publishing it.

4. Grammarly

Grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text. It has several features that make it useful for improving writing, including:

Pros:

  • Checks for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text
  • Provides suggestions for improving clarity, concision, and readability
  • Can be integrated with various apps and platforms such as Microsoft Office, Google Docs, and social media platforms
  • Offers a browser extension and a desktop app
  • Has a premium version with more advanced features such as plagiarism detection and more

Cons:

  • The suggestions provided may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The grammar checker may not always recognize context-specific language use
  • The free version has limited features

#9785. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”

#9779. What is piloncillo? This sweetener makes great cookies, pan dulce, and more: Use this traditional Mexican unrefined sugar for a dash of flavor and history.

This article is part of our feature celebrating Pan Dulce. Find all things pan dulce here.

Categorically, piloncillo is a “non-centrifugal” cane sugar, meaning it is an unrefined sugar product and a true natural brown sugar. It’s mostly consumed in Mexico and Latin America, but a similar product can be found in Asia, known as jaggery in India. Though often lumped together, these unrefined dark sugars are very different from brown sugars on the market today, which have been refined to a large degree — in some cases, they’re actually just white sugar with coloring or molasses added.

Making piloncillo, on the other hand, involves an artisanal process that’s hundreds of years old. To make it, pressed cane juice is boiled to evaporate the water and deeply caramelize the sugar. The cooked cane is then poured into molds (often made of wood) and left to dry and harden. Traditional piloncillo is conical in shape and can vary in size from small to large cones but is most commonly found in a medium size that weighs about 200 grams. In Guatemala and Colombia, it is called panela, where it is cooked to a lighter degree and typically formed into a brick, rather than cone, shape. Other forms of piloncillo can be granulated or liquid (which is more rare).

Minimally processed and boldly flavored, piloncillo was historically a prized and respected foodstuff. As an unrefined cane sugar, piloncillo provides more complex vitamins and minerals than refined sugars, which undergo processing and whitening methods that also strip nutrients from the whole food. And piloncillo is also great for baking, providing notes of burnt caramel and hints of smoke. Plus, its rich molasses qualities keep baked goods moist and fresh for longer.

Always look at the ingredient label when purchasing piloncillo and make sure it says 100% pure cane juice or cane sugar. It is becoming increasingly common to find imitation products marketed as jaggery or piloncillo that contain coloring and corn syrup. You can find good piloncillo at specialty grocery stores or online at retailers.

In Mexico and throughout Latin America, piloncillo is an important ingredient in many traditional dishes. (Some will even say it’s not the “real dish” if you substitute sugar in these recipes due to the deep flavors and richness that only piloncillo can provide.) This deep, dark unrefined sugar lends its characteristic flavor and texture to popular foods and beverages such as capirotada, tepache, coyotas, atole, café de olla, calabaza al horno, coricos, and hojarascas, to name a few!

I love adding piloncillo when I’m making champurrado. In this warm and thick chocolate beverage, the piloncillo is chopped or grated and dissolved in the pot with water or milk before adding the chocolate and masa. In this recipe, the piloncillo’s intense sweet and smoky flavors pair well with the chocolate and corn masa.

While there are many dishes and uses for piloncillo, it’s not a simple substitution for granulated white sugar in recipes, but you can use it the same as you would brown sugar with a 1:1 substitution by weight.  Depending on how hard the cone is, it can be crumbled or grated for easier measuring. If it is very hard, try cutting it in half with a sharp knife and then placing it between parchment paper or a towel and beating with a rolling pin.

Find puerquitos and many more Mexican sweets in our feature celebrating pan dulce.

#9777. Add This Fresh Herb To Your Bowl Of Chili For 10x The Flavor (Thanks, Ina Garten)

A bowl of chili welcomes a wide array of renditions. You can make the dish red or green, use proteins like turkey, pork, or chicken instead of the classic beef, and include many aromatics in the mix. Each detail makes a chili rendition unique. Even a fresh herb gives a bowl a whole new character — just look toward Ina Garten's inclusion of basil. Ina Garten often uses basil as a swap for cilantro, so her inclusion of the herb in her chili makes sense.

Using the Mediterranean herb in the Tex-Mex recipe may sound unusual, but the flavors align surprisingly well. Garten uses basil's mildly citrusy sweet and lightly peppery flavor specifically in a chicken-based chili, integrating the herb during both the initial simmering stage and as a final garnish. It's a one-two combo that establishes an herbal character that infuses into every bite, lending more than just a basil-inflected finish.

Garten's rendition works the basil into a tomato sauce base, full of sweet bell peppers and onions, lightly recalling a pasta sauce in composition. Still, seasonings like cumin, chili powder, and a dash of spicy cayenne appear in the mix, cementing the dish as a bowl of chili, only brighter and more herbal in nature.

Ina Garten's tips for cooking chicken perfectly dependably deliver, but don't rule out employing the basil in chili recipes with other proteins, too. The herb also works well in an extra-hearty bean and brisket rendition that's spiced with chiles and even coffee. Cooked down right alongside the kidney beans, basil lends the legumes its distinct herbal character, all without becoming a cornerstone flavor. You can try out such a technique in a classic ground beef chili, too; using the herb early in cooking makes it one of many layered flavors.

If you're after a more basil-forward spin, consider working the herb into a ground turkey chili recipe. You can still go heavy on the spice, using chili powder and jalapeños alongside garlic powder and cumin. Add dried basil early on and raw basil atop the finished chili, and you'll get a delicate bowl, herbal-tasting and fresh, yet still pretty classic.

And for a more inventive approach, take a page from Thai cuisine, specifically Phat ka-phrao (stir-fried basil beef). Made with sturdier Thai basil, this version of the herb stands up better to heat. Saute the meat alongside extra-spicy chiles, lots of garlic, and this type of basil, and you can lay down the foundation for an extra-bold chili, still delicious over rice or with tortilla chips.

#9774. Two Personality Traits Linked To A Sharper Mind

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

Intellectual curiosity and an appreciation of beauty are both linked to stronger thinking skills.

People with these qualities tend to perform better on tests of literacy, numeracy and problem-solving.

The findings suggest that a person’s interest in ideas and aesthetic experiences may offer clues to their cognitive abilities.

Curiosity could encourage people to seek out opportunities to learn, while stronger thinking skills could make exploring complex ideas more rewarding, with both processes reinforcing one another.

Intellectual curiosity involves enjoying ideas, wanting to understand things and being drawn to questions that require thought.

Aesthetic sensitivity describes an appreciation of art and beauty.

Both qualities belong to the broader personality trait of openness to experience, which captures how receptive people are to unfamiliar ideas and experiences.

However, openness also includes creative imagination, and this aspect showed no significant independent association with cognitive performance.

Imagination, curiosity and an appreciation of beauty may overlap in everyday life, but their relationships with thinking skills differ.

The conclusions come from an analysis of almost 68,000 people across 12 countries, including Canada, Germany, Italy and New Zealand.

They completed personality questionnaires alongside assessments of literacy, numeracy and the ability to solve problems as circumstances change.

Intellectual curiosity and aesthetic sensitivity were linked to better performance across all three assessments, even after accounting for other personality traits.

The connections between personality and cognitive skills also varied between countries.

Educational systems and cultural practices could help explain such differences, although the reasons remain uncertain.

Overall, the findings link both a desire to understand the world and an appreciation of its beauty with stronger thinking skills.

The study was published in the journal Large-scale Assessments in Education (Rammstedt et al., 2026).

Tuna salad is a pragmatic yet delicious dish, easily crafted using pantry staples. Open up some canned fish packed in oil or water, mix with store-bought mayo, then fold in some aromatics, and you'll have yourself a tasty classic. It's a tried-and-true formula that welcomes many other shelf-stable components, like panko bread crumbs, for example. You only need about 2 tablespoons per can of tuna to round things out nicely.

The delicate breadcrumb style is wonderfully versatile in the kitchen, and its texture enhances tuna salad, too. The foodstuff lends the dish more body, without turning it too dense. The panko absorbs moisture, making the crumbs turn soft while still retaining airiness, in turn creating an extra-tender salad. The panko also thickens the dish, giving your meal more structure. Not to mention, a bite here or there might still remain crunchy, upping the textural intrigue.

It's an advantageous set of qualities unique specifically to panko; you won't want to reach for a different breadcrumb in this application, as they may be too dense. This Japanese foodstuff is made using a unique electric cooking process, producing a delicate crumble without any bread crust. Other breadcrumb varieties are simply too heavy for the task. So grab a package of panko online or in stores to make a tuna salad rendition with a textural twist.

Not sure how to round out a tuna salad with panko? The options are wide-ranging. You could keep to a straightforward mix of tuna, mayo, salt, and pepper — perfect for a tuna sandwich filling — or go with the many potential tuna salad upgrades. Walnuts or kimchi, for example, add body and even more texture to the dish.

Alternatively, consider playing to the breadcrumb's East Asian origins, using other Japanese ingredients in the dish. Or go down the spicy tuna route, incorporating a hot sauce like Sriracha into the build — especially tasty when wrapped in seaweed. Swap the standard mayo for a Japanese-style emulsion, mix in the panko, and you'll have yourself a magical tuna salad foundation.

#9769. Scrambled Eggs Get A Major Protein And Flavor Boost When You Add This Omega-Rich Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

When many of us think "hot breakfast," we tend to naturally gravitate toward thoughts of scrambled eggs. Aside from the fact that, when prepared correctly, they are tender, delicate, and fluffy (or custardy, depending on how you like them), eggs are considered the gold standard for protein, so they are quite wholesome as well. On their own, though, they can get a little monotonous, especially if you're making them every day, so it does help to add an ingredient here or there. And if you happen to enjoy omega-3-rich cold-smoked salmon, well, it pairs seamlessly with a classic scramble, boosting both the flavor and the protein content.

Once considered an expensive delicacy, smoked salmon is quite popular now in the U.S., and as a result, it's much easier to find at your local grocery store (even Aldi carries its own version, and it can be found at Walmart, too). Cold-smoked salmon, despite the fact that it tends to be packed in super-thin slices, is buttery and velvety. While it does taste fishy, there are also light, smoky notes that give it a deeply savory flavor, which works beautifully when combined with the mild egg scramble. Additionally, a serving (which will vary in size) might contain anywhere from 12 to 18 grams of protein, which is great if you have daily goals you want to meet or you're just looking to get more of the macronutrient in general.

Truly, the most difficult part about incorporating smoked salmon into your scramble is cooking the eggs to the right consistency without burning or browning them. All you have to do with the salmon is slice the ultra-thin pieces into slivers or small squares. Once your eggs have reached the texture you desire, you'll take the pan off the heat and fold in the salmon. That's literally it; you don't have to actually cook the salmon over direct heat because it's so delicate that the residual warmth of the scrambled eggs will gently bring it up to temperature.

Now, because smoked salmon is so light and thin, you might want your eggs to match that energy, so create a fluffy, soft texture with a bit of cream whisked in. Alternatively, you could take a page out of Bobby Flay's book and fold in a dollop of crème fraîche, or really up the decadence and melt in some cubes of cream cheese (and take care not to overcook anything, because smoked salmon with burnt, rubbery eggs? No thanks). Also, because all of the elements involved are either rich or thick, a sprinkling of something green, like fresh chives or dill, or even a little parsley or tarragon, would brighten things up, both aesthetically and in terms of flavor.

#9766. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

#9765. Forget Expensive Ribeye: A Cheaper Cut For Delicious Beef Stroganoff

Indulgently and immensely comforting, beef stroganoff is one of those low-effort meals you make when you just want to feel good. But one thing that might not lift your spirits is the price. Classic stroganoff starts off with strips of thinly sliced beef, with cuts like ribeye being among the best picks. We're not here to fault ribeye, which has earned its price for a reason, but if you want to knock a few dollars off your next batch, try swapping in ground beef instead.

While it may not satisfy the purist, and might even horrify a Russian (the dish's country of origin), we'd argue that ground beef is a worthy alternative to any traditional whole cut of steak. The texture is bound to be different, and you'll need to adjust how you cook it, but good-quality ground beef still has the rich, beefy flavor that pairs so well with the tang of sour cream, earthy mushrooms, and the sweet depth of cooked-down onions, all at a significantly lower cost.

Another reason ground beef works so well here is its cooking time. Traditional beef stroganoff relies on expensive cuts that are prized for their tenderness and quick-cooking nature. Cheaper, tougher cuts like chuck or round usually need hours of braising to soften, which doesn't suit a dish that's meant to come together quickly. Ground beef, however, is often made from those same economical cuts, and the grinding process does all the tenderizing mechanically. That means you're getting all that mouthwatering flavor without the waiting, guaranteeing a tasty, Boomer-approved meal.

If you make the switch from ribeye to ground beef, you'll want to do a few things differently. First, check out the numbers on your ground beef packaging. You're looking for a blend that doesn't shy away from fat, something like an 80-to-20 lean-to-fat ratio, or even 70-to-30. Like ribeye, these fattier blends are packed with rich flavor, and the fat that'll render out will elevate the sauce, just in a different format. Go any leaner and you risk dry, chewy beef pebbles floating in your sauce.

With ribeye, standard practice is to slice the beef ultra-thin, give it a quick sear, then let it simmer in the sauce for a few minutes. The process for ground beef is similar, albeit with a few caveats. For starters, there's no slicing, so you're already saving time. Like ribeye, you want to get the meat nicely browned. Our personal advice is to add the beef to the pan in small handfuls and flatten each one with the back of a spoon, which allows it to brown without overcrowding the pan.

Remove the beef from the pan once it's seared, which isn't usually done with ribeye. Even in a fattier blend, ground beef has far more exposed surface area than your average slice of steak, so it risks drying out if it's left to simmer for too long. For the most tender results, build your sauce first, then add the beef back in and stir once you're just about ready to serve. Don't worry about the flavors not melding, since the fat and fond left behind from searing will be doing most of the heavy lifting.
